speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ME. GRAYDON-FREEDOM OF SPEECH IN THE PARLIAMENT OF CANADA
speechtext:
I desire to rise to a question of privilege. It relates to certain strong protests which have been made recently in parliament, as well as outside, with respect to the right of freedom of speech in the parliament of Canada. I have delayed bringing up this matter in the House of Commons in the expectation that the government leader in the other place, or the member around whom the issue revolved, would introduce the matter on a question of privilege in the other chamber when it reconvened on Tuesday last after having been in adjournment almost continuously since the incident occurred. In view of the fact that the question has not been raised in the other place, however, I am bringing it now before this house since it concerns the rights of members of both branches of parliament. In my opinion the inalienable right of freedom of speech which must be enjoyed by every member of parliament, whether in the other place, the House of Commons or any other deliberative assembly in Canada, should be zealously safeguarded and vigorously defended.
Without making further comment with respect to the matter I am going to ask the Prime Minister, who is not in his place at the moment, in view of the fact that the situation affects both houses of parliament, if he will call into conference with him the leader of the government in the senate so that the matter may be fully reviewed and such steps taken in both houses simultaneously as may be felt necessary to ensure that freedom of speech shall be maintained and preserved.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: FLOOR PRICE FOR ONTARIO WHEAT, 1944-45 CROP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the

permission of the house I should like to make a brief statement of considerable urgency, so far as Ontario wheat farmers are concerned.
I wish to announce that the government has decided to provide a floor price for Ontario wheat during the 1944-45 crop year. The Canadian wheat board has been empowered to purchase in terminal market positions No. 1 grades of Ontario winter wheat at $1.25 per bushel, basis Montreal.
It is the hope of the government that Ontario winter wheat will be purchased by mills at the ceiling price during the present ;rop year, and that it will not be necessary for he board to purchase wheat in volume in order to guarantee a minimum price of $1.25 per bushel for No. 1 grades, Montreal basis. However, should prices weaken, or should supplies of Ontario wheat offered for sale during the crop year exceed requirements of eastern mills, the board will exercise the special powers granted to it for the present crop year and will maintain minimum prices on the basis of $1.25 per bushel for No. 1 grades, basis Montreal.
In so far as the board becomes a purchaser of Ontario winter wheat in 1944-45 it will do so in respect to standard grades of wheat in store in terminal elevators and will do so as a market stabilization measure. Any loss resulting from board operations in this respect will be a charge upon the treasury.
I wish to point out that this stabilization measure will be operated in the place of an initial advance to producers with participation certificates hitherto provided under the Canadian Wheat Board Act. With the ceiling at SI.26, it is the considered opinion of the government that Ontario winter wheat producers will realize more from the support of the terminal market prices of their wheat than under the system of producer deliveries to the board which was formerly in effect.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Provided that the committee agree; but I must ask the committee to keep the discussion within the ambit of the item before the committee.

With the consent of the committee we will take up 409o and see what can be done about it. This item includes storage batteries, and it is most interesting. I should like to go back to 1935 when Mr. Bennett was Prime Minister and show the committee what the duty on storage batteries was at that time. I am interested in this because in many country places where no power is available the farmers rely upon storage batteries for a great many things and they are a little handicapped in their purchases. I will tell the committee what handicaps the rural class of this country.
In 1935 there was a distinction between electric and galvanic batteries, the ordinary storage battery. A change is now being made in the designation of the item. Previously the tariff was most complicated. For electric and galvanic batteries the British preferential tariff was 15 per cent; the most favoured nation, 25 per cent; intermediate, 25 per cent and general, 27i per cent. Listen to this description of "battery" that is given. The term used was not general, it was specific and it made the thing most complicated. Listen to this:
Batteries, storage electric, composed of plates measuring not less than 11 inches 'by 14 inches
Customs Tariff

and not less than three-quarters of an inch in thickness, and complete parts thereof: free; 25; 25; 27|.
The rates given are for the British preferential, most favoured nation, intermediate and general. I wonder if that description was put there to protect the manufacturers of storage batteries. All other electric and galvanic batteries were 15, 25, 25 and 27J. There was a distinction made between the two kinds of batteries. That was the tariff that existed in 1935 and it continued until 1940, but now it is being changed. We now have storage batteries under item 409o, which reads:
Equipment for generating electric power for farm purposes only, viz: engine, gas tank, generator, storage battery, and switchboard or panel; and complete parts of the foregoing: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.
The most favoured nation tariff has disappeared. The explanatory note does not mention what the tariff is now, but according to the information I have it is free, 25, 25 and 27 J. The description here is most vague. All the items are put together and it is most difficult to find out what we want in the tariff. We have to refer to a book that is published outside of our government, the "Canadian Almanac" which lists all the tariff items alphabetically. I suppose the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue maintain their own alphabetical indexes, but the members of parliament are not provided with a copy, and when they want information about the tariff they have to go to the excellent compilation made by the "Canadian Almanac". That means, strangely enough, that if we want information on the tariff we have to rely on publications outside of the government unless we wish to go through a whole lot of work. That is one point.
What will be the effect of this reduction on imports? Before the war it was easy for anyone to send $100 or $500 to the United States, or to England or anywhere else, to obtain storage batteries. Tt is not possible to do that now except with the authorization of the foreign exchange control board. I am all for a reduction in the tariff on this item, but because of the autocracy of the foreign exchange control board it is impossible for the farmers to get any batteries from the United States. They cannot take advantage of this tariff reduction to secure what they need. I remember that a long time ago a committee of this house sat and considered the duties on agricultural implements and brought in a report recommending a decrease in duties, but nothing was done about that unit! now; and now, when it is done, it is to no purpose. That is

my complaint. So long as the farmers are handicapped in getting what they need, by the regulations of the foreign exchange control board, it is impossible for them to take advantage of this reduction in the tariff. The same thing applies to exports. It is impossible to export because of the export restrictions. What is the use of the export permit branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce? They cannot do anything. They are under the control of the controllers of the Department of Munitions and Supply and under the wartime prices and trade board. That is the position, and it means that traders are tied up.
Some storage batteries are manufactured in Canada, but it is essential that our farmers have access to an open market in the United States to buy their batteries there because they are not well served by the firms in Toronto, who always serve wholesalers before serving the small dealers in country places. I had to bother the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance a number of times over numerous and justified complaints with respect to the radio service in Temiscouata county. We have a very good service there under an excellent man, but it is impossible for him to get the materials he requires from the manufacturer or from the wholesaler. That is another reason why the matter should be considered in connection with this tariff item which we are now considering. The perfect radio service of Temiscouata should have the opportunity to order as many storage batteries as they need to supply the farmers of my district without going to the manufacturers in Toronto, who do not give them the service to which they are entitled. It is as clear as crystal. The tariff item itself is good, and I do not oppose it. Once more I say that I am opposing the restrictions imposed by the Department of Finance through the foreign exchange control board, which make these tariff provisions perfectly useless.
I have the highest regard for the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who I believe is a great collaborator with the Minister of Finance, but the Minister of Finance should not have ail this power in his hands through the various organizations which are under his control. How is it that the British preferential tariff has been left for so long at fifteen per cent on electric and galvanic batteries? It was impossible to secure batteries f-om the United Kingdom and yet this government is the one that is preaching patriotism. They say their heart is with Great Britain, but when it comes down to brass tacks there has been a fifteen per cent tariff for so long on British goods. I have done some research but

Customs Tariff
I did not have the time to examine the whole record between 1940 and 1944. I realize, however, that it waa only after a long time that the tariff was changed.
I might give the names of some of the Toronto firms which are most unsatisfactory, and one gentleman who knows all about it is precisely the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, with whom I have dealt regarding these matters. It is impossible to get any satisfaction from these Toronto firms. When one of my constituents sent a Toronto firm an accepted cheque it was returned and the firm did not fill the order. The parliamentary assistant then got in touch with the firm in Toronto, through one of the controllers, and notified them that in all fairness they should serve my constituents in a better way. But what did they get? They got what they wanted drop by drop, only a very small quantity at a time. During all that time the farmers were suffering on account of the stupidity of these people. I am against manufacturers having the power to control the exports of any other manufacturer, or to control the imports of any other manufacturer. So long as the various organizations under the department of finance are not submitted to the control of parliament, we shall get nowhere.
There is another thing I want to say. I am greatly concerned about the way in which tariffs are made. I go back to April 6, 1936, when I made this motion in the house. I quote from Hansard of April 6, 1936, page 1815:
Mr. Pouliot moved for a copy of the last draft of the Canadian American agreement as it was on October 23, 1935.
Mr. Mackenzie King: I am not aware that there is a draft of any Canada-United States agreement dated October 23. 1935. If there is. I think it would be a privileged document and as such could not properly be brought down.
Mr. Bennett:	It has been distinctly stated
that there was no such draft.
Mr. Pouliot: Then nothing was done by the previous administration in that connection.
Motion dropped.
My point was not so much that the Bennett government, through Mr. Herridge's negotiations with the United States government, had done nothing, but rather that this government took office on October 21, 1935, and, the Canada-United States trade agreement was entered into at Washington three weeks after, on November 15. [DOT] What wizards! Is it possible for any man on earth to make a treaty in three weeks when nothing has been done before? There was no agreement as to any item of the tariff at the time. Now, sir,
they are precisely the people who boss the whole show, and it is impossible to criticize them and they are above all of us.
My conclusion is this. The controllers, the wartime prices and trade board, the foreign exchange control board-if these are to subsist any longer, to the detriment of the Canadian people, they should be told definitely by the Minister of Finance that the needs of the Canadian people should be looked after, and merely because a man lives in the country he should not be deprived of the advantages which a man who lives in the city has. Every Canadian citizen has the right to the same facilities and the same comfort, but until now, through the stupidity and greed of the manufacturers of batteries in the cities of Toronto and Montreal, the Canadian farmer has been deprived of storage batteries. Many a time when he asked for a battery he could not get it because it was easier to fill larger orders.
It is a simple matter for the minister to avoid a lot of useless correspondence by giving formal orders, in the first place, to the wartime prices and trade board, and in the second place to the foreign exchange control board, to impose no restriction on the import of such goods. He should also notify the Canadian manufacturers that if they do not serve the country people as they deserve to be served, the foreign exchange control board will allow the Canadian merchants who sell batteries in rural districts to buy all they need from the United States, and give them the right to send money to the United States to buy those batteries.
It is not mjr desire to handicap the Canadian manufacturer; on the other hand, if the Canadian manufacturer is not serving the Canadian people it is the duty of the government to redress that wrong; and the government must be obeyed, too. It is very easy for them to do that.
Besides that, the Minister of Munitions and Supply should not miss an opportunity to tell the chief of controls-successor to one who was connected for a long time with Barclay's bank and is now one of the numerous heads of the Tory party, namely Harry Borden:- that he should do nothing to give privileges to the big dealers in the cities at the expense of the smaller dealers in rural communities. It is easy to do that. If the respective controllers-Donald Gordon, of the wartime prices and trade board, or L. Rasminsky, of the exchange control board, and the rest- do not obey the minister, out they go; the minister can fire them at any time, because, I assume, they are there "during pleasure"

I use the words "during pleasure" because that is the term which is used most of the time in connection with appointments, but it should be interpreted as meaning "during good service". So long as the storage battery man is dealt with in that manner, to serve the few instead of the many, the system cannot work at all, and these organizations should be condemned severely and bitterly. I am sure that all hon. members who represent rural communities agree with me in this matter. I hope they will say so to the minis

With regard to the wartime prices and trade board, the hon. gentleman suggested that that board or the Department of Munitions and Supply were in some way restricting quotas. Now so far as imports are concerned the whole object of the wartime prices and trade board is to secure as generous quotas as possible from the United States, and they have administrative machinery set up for that purpose. They never cut down quotas for protective purposes; they seek to enlarge

quotas so as to ensure adequate civilian .supply. They are the agency of the government charged with the responsibility for civilian supply.
With regard to adequate domestic supply, that depends upon wartime necessity. If materials and labour are required for war purposes it may be necessary to restrict the amount of materials at least that can go into the production of civilian equipment and civilian supply. That is a matter primarily under the jurisdiction of the war industries control board in the Department of Munitions and Supply; but so far as the agencies in my department are concerned they seek continually to get as large or as nearly adequate amounts for civilian supply as is possible under the circumstances. They have two duties, one in respect of supply and the second in respect of prices and the control of prices, dependent upon their provision of an adequate civilian supply. The hon. gentleman can depend upon it that so far as the agencies in my department are concerned, they will do the best they can to see that civilians are adequately supplied.

Item 71 covers the building
of fishways and clearing of rivers, and I have two items about which I wish to speak briefly. I can put them both on the record at the same time and the minister can answer them together. The first one refers to a fish ladder on the Puntledge river a few miles from the town of Courtenay in British Columbia. This river leads into Comox lake where for many years there was a good run of valuable salmon. This run has practically ceased. The committee will not be interested in the whole history of this matter. It is an unsavoury one so far as certain government officials are concerned. I have a huge file on it, larger than the ordinary volumes of the debates of the house. Unless the minister is prepared to challenge my statements there will be no need to' go into it in detail. It did not occur during his time so that he is not responsible in any way.
The case goes back to 1913 when a colliery company wanted to obtain power and put in a dam on the Puntledge river. Sometimes it takes a long time for the government to take action or for the people to stir up the government, but it was finally discovered that this dam was ruining the run of salmon into that lake. Along about 1917 the public agitated

Supply-Fisheries
about it and continued to do so until I came into the house in 1921. In 1922 the government ordered the company to put in a fish ladder at that point, that being the law. For some reason which I need not go into, the company was allowed to put in the wrong type of fish ladder and it was washed out before long. The government compelled the company to .put in another. The same type of fish ladder was put in at the same place and it was washed out again. That happened once, twice, three times. It finally dawned on the officials that perhaps there was something wrong in the procedure. In order to make things quite comfortable and amicable all around they ordered a new type of ladder to be put, in, but it was put in the wrong place. It had the additional disadvantage that even though the ladder was there the fish could not use it The fish could at least get up the former ladders when they were there. But on this occasion, in order to make a gesture of doing something, they put in a different type of ladder which was of no value even for the comparatively short time it was there before it too was washed out. The last washout occurred in December, 1937.
I charged the officials with the responsibility for doing that. By this time I may say that the colliery company, very naturally to my mind, took the position that they had put in the ladder which they did not want to do, that it was of no advantage to them but that that was the law; they had put it in three times and if the government had no more sense than to keep on putting it in in the wrong place and putting in the wrong type, that was up to the government and they would not be responsible any further. I think that was an entirely proper stand for them to take. I maintained at that time, and I have since, that the responsibility was the government's, first, to do it; second, to put in a type that would be practical and, third, to put it in in a place and in a manner where it would stay.
Of course officials of the government will never take the blame for anything if they have done anything wrong. They will go through hell and high water rather than admit that they have made a mistake. They would not take any blame and they offered) various excuses to justify the action they had taken. First of all they said that it was working all right, that the fish were getting up. I said it was not, and I brought evidence to show that it was not. After the usual official delay they went to the expense of putting in a net above the fish ladder in order to demonstrate that the fish were getting up; they intended to catch the fish and demonstrate that I was wrong. They did not catch anything, they did) not even
catch a sucker, or at all events not the sucker they thought they were going to catch.
The next argument was: Yes, that was so, but it was impossible to put in a ladder in that peculiar position to get the fish over the dam, which was eleven feet high at the most. But we have evidence before us of salmon having been taken up the Columbia river at Bonneville falls, a height of sixty feet, without any of these desperate troubles that afflicted them here.
When that was dissipated they got a new idea. The next idea was that it could not be put where common sense would suggest at the end of the dam because that would require blasting and would involve the safety of the dam. That was a childish argument. I have blasted a stump within six feet of the windows of my house without damaging the glass. It requires judicious care, of course. We finally got a couple of first-class engineers and they said that the ladder should be put, not in the middle of the dam where it would be under such pressure that it would not work-and when it did work it was speedily washed out- but at the end of it, and that would need some blasting. That was the advice of two very competent engineers.
The next argument was this. They were determined that the ladder would not be put in and they would not admit that they had made a mistake. That is a trait of human character, I suppose, but it can be pushed to an extent in the official mind. The next argument was that the fish did not go up there anyway, and never had, so what was the use of putting in a ladder? But they put in the first one in 1922. They put in altogether four ladders, and they were all washed out, and now they said there was no need for a ladder at all because the fish had never been up there. I mention that just to illustrate the mental attitude with which I had to contend. The records of the department-I leave it to the minister, although it is not his responsibility-are full of recommendations from the government side by various officials. One man who had a long and established career in such matters said that it was the finest place for spawning fish that he had seen in British Columbia. Yet their argument was that the fish had never gone up there, and therefore there was no need for a ladder.
You can imagine that all these things took time. All these excuses had to be combated. Finally, just about the time that I was hoping for some action, the war broke out and it was put up to me as a patriotic gesture, and as common sense too, that this was not a pressing war emergency and it had better not be gone on with for the present. I accepted that view
Supply-Fisheries

and did not put on any more pressure. That is how it stands now. But now, if we can credit the morning newspapers, we are getting close to the end of the war. We can now look forward, and it is highly undesirable that we should let this matter stand any longer, for of course the run of the fish is getting smaller and smaller, if indeed it exists at all. Looking to the future I think it would be desirable if the government would give its consent now to - putting a sum in the supplementary estimates to meet the expenditure for this work. It would not require a very large sum, five or six thousand dollars, not much more than that. I am shortly leaving politics entirely, but I have been pressing this matter through the years and I would like to see it brought to a satisfactory conclusion.
The other matter that I wish to bring up has to do with this same vote, in connection with the clearing of creeks and rivers. This is a different situation. The government in times past spent over five thousand dollars to allow the salmon to get up the Rosewall creek. Their object, and their sole object in making this expenditure, is to see that the salmon do get up, and they do not care what the consequences are to anyone else who happens to be affected. That is not a reasonable method. They spent five thousand dollars, and most of it was spent in an attack, so to speak, on a big log jam which had come down and settled in a place where there were high banks on each side, and consequently it did not make a lot of difference to anybody except the salmon whether the logs piled up there or not. I forget whether they cut the jam or blasted it. I think they cut a hole or tunnel through this log jam, through which the salmon got up temporarily, at any rate, until other things happened. Cutting the jam had what we call consequential results. Cutting off a piece of the log jam allowed the next freshet to swing the jam around and carry lit down a few hundred yards, where the logs all jammed again on a bar, a flat place where there were no high banks as before. The logs jammed on this bar in a low flat place and stayed there, and subsequent logs coming down kept on piling up. The consequence was that the water spread out over this flat land in the neighbourhood and ruined the land. As we all know, delta land is the very best land you can get for farming, and it does not have to be cleared. Settlers had taken up land on both sides of this flat, but the log jam, being stuck there, piled up more and more in the course of the years and in time it got so bad that the creek sometimes disappears into the gravel and comes out lower down, but that is under exceptional circumstances. The

result was that water and silt spread over this flat land; the farm land is being ruined, and the usefulness of the river as a salmon spawning ground is also gone. The salmon would get up with the big freshet and lie on the flat ground, and when the freshet went out they were stranded and the young salmon would lie in little holes; they stayed there until the creek dried up, and the fish perished. So that the run of salmon is entirely rained.
These settlers went to the department which had caused the damage, because it is the department's responsibility. If any department does something with one object in view, and it causes a loss to somebody else, that, is the department's responsibility. That has been admitted time and again, although reluctantly, by the department. But they took an attitude in this case that reminds me of Judas Iscariot. After he had taken the step of which he later repented-at any rate he had the merit of having repented, and these officials have not-he went to the priests and gave them back the money, or he wanted to. He said: I have shed innocent blood and I want to return the money. But the priests said: No; what is that to us? See thou to it. That is the attitude taken by the officials. They said to these struggling settlers whose land had been ruined: What is that to us? See thou to it. That attitude is against common law and against common sense and that sense of fairness which should animate any department in such matters.
That is well quoted and well applied.

Then they say, "Well; all these other things have happened, it is not worth our spending any more money anyhow." They put forth the same specious arguments which I have alluded to in the other matter. First of all they said they never did spend any money. I have a letter to that effect. But it is well known that they spent five thousand dollars, or near that. Then they said it did not do any harm anyhow;, this log jam would have done the same thing in any case. No, it would not, because it was jammed between high banks where nothing would have happened, or if it had happened it would have been higher up the creek where it did not matter. But by their action, cutting a hole through or a piece off the edge of the jam, it allowed the whole thing to float down, and it jammed on this flat river basin with the results I have indicated.
Then they tell us that the erosion had nothing to do with them, they were not responsible for erosion, the creek cutting down

Supply-Fisheries
the bank; and they said it was up to the province or, if it was not up to the province, it was up to the individual, who must suffer from being affected by that disability. But in this particular case it was not an act of Providence or of nature; it was the act of the officials of the fisheries department carrying out their duties in attempting to let the salmon up. The log jam when it stranded diverted the current and caused the erosion. It was this which made the trouble, and therefore the settlers, I maintain, have the right to come to the department to do something about it.
The next argument was that it would cost so much money; it would cost ten thousand dollars, and ten thousand dollars was a lot of money to spend on what some people may think is a two-penny-ha'penny creek. But it will not cost ten thousand dollars. I am going to read a letter from one of the persons concerned who would undertake to remedy the condition for eight hundred or a thousand dollars, and make a good job of it, and would be satisfied to release the government from all claims. I intend to read some letters which explain what damage has been done. Some of the land belongs to a widow woman. She has had five or six acres of her land ruined, worth three or four hundred dollars an acre of any man's money. Land has been either washed away or rendered utterly useless, and I contend that these people are entitled to redress.
I do not want the government to take advantage of the technicalities of the law and say, like the priests of old, "What is that to us?" It is everything to these people; and the government is supposed to exhibit an example of fair play. I would not be a bit afraid, if I or this man had the money, to take this matter into the exchequer court, for I have a pretty good idea of what that court would do, but the man has not any money to spend on an action in the exchequer court, and of course the officials take the view that they can afford to bluff this thing through.
In substantiation of some of the statements which I have made, I am going to read extracts from letters. I have enough here to go on reading for a couple of hours, because this condition has existed for a long time, but I intend to read only a few extracts in confirmation of the statements I have made. If the minister would spend a sum not exceeding S750 probably the man and other parties associated with him would be glad to accept it in settlement. I quote from a letter of a friend of mine who lives nearby and is cognizant of the situation:
Considerable amount of property has been washed away. This is caused by a huge log jam which has accumulated causing the creek to spread all over the place and cause considerable amount of damage. The gravel below the log jam is piled higher than the banks. This log jam has completely blocked the creek. There is no creek bed; the water seeps away through the gravel. In the spring as the mouth of this creek dried up small pools of water were left full of fish. Thousands of them were trapped and eaten by cranes, crows, gulls, etc. Salmon go up this creek to spawn. As a spawning bed for salmon I feel that the fisheries department should remove this obstruction known as the huge log jam in Rosewall creek.
Here is a letter from one of the parties concerned; his name is Curran:
I am taking this opportunity to write you again to ask you if you will try and do something at Ottawa to have the mouth of Rosewall cleaned out. If you recollect I took this matter up with you several years ago and you visited my place and saw the condition of this river for yourself. The truth of the matter is all the damage done in Rosewall creek has been caused by the fishery department itself.
In 1935 the fishery department cut a channel to allow the fish to get past a large jam about a mile and a half upstream from the mouth of the river. The first flood after the channel was cut swung this jam down intact to the mouth of the river where it lodged, backing up the sand and gravel and other log jams which came down there by filling up the river bed and forcing the water to run all over my fields and the land adjoining us.
Here is another letter from him. He says that the officials have been to look at his place [DOT]-the continued efforts I made brought them to this easily accessible place. It was all part of a "stall". The fisheries department is fuller of "stalls" than a livery stable. He says that the officials have been to his place, and adds:
I would suggest if possible that you check these reports. I believe their estimates run between three and four thousand dollars to put this creek back to its natural state, and that is probably the reason why the fishery department is sidetracking the issue, on account of the high cost. However, if it is at all possible to get an appropriation of between eight hundred to one thousand dollars I will guarantee to put the creek back to its natural state and make a good job of it and will pay the balance out of my own pocket.
Notice what he asks: he wants it put back to where it was to begin with, its natural state. The fact that it has been a complete failure from the point of view of the salmon getting up is nothing to him, naturally. What he thinks about is that the land for which he paid a high price cannot now be used.
Here is another letter, from the widow, Mrs. Berray. She is addressing my friend:
Fred Curran, Art Smith, and myself went up to the highway bridge on Rosewall creek and came all the way down the creek and we counted 85 dead salmon down as far as the big [DOT] log jam. Below that there are thousands that never got past the log jam. When there is a

it would be as well to let nature take its course. The stream will eventually scour into a new well defined outlet to the sea, hut in doing so the greater part of the cleared farmland at its mouth will most likely be washed away, or be ruined by erosion and scouring.
Now that is not an ex parte statement at all: it is not my statement but an official's statement. Different reports have been sub-

mitted to the minister upon which he is relying, and I have just read from an official statement. Here is another, signed J. McHugh, the resident engineer employed by the fisheries department for many years, a man of outstanding ability in his line, and one whose professional reputation would prevent him from making statements which he did not believe to be accurate. Mr. McHugh says:
There is no obstruction to the ascent of salmon at the mouth of Rosewall creek but there is quite an extensive jam from 80 to 100 feet long occupying the entire bed of the stream about one-quarter mile upstream, and it would appear an effort should be made to clear a channel around this jam on the south bank.
He goes on to say that even for temporary clearance they should spend $100 in that particular year, which was 1940. In this connection he says that the sum of $100-
-will be required for this temporary clearance which will take care of the salmon run this season. Additional work will in all probability be necessary from year to year on this stream.
That $100 was not spent, and in fact they have done nothing since then except talk. That is the situation. While it is unfortunate that public money should have been spent, I do not blame them in that case. They did what I perhaps woutd have done if it had been left to me to try to remove the log jam; but instead of tinkering with it I would have seen to it that the whole jam was blasted or burned out. It would all have gone. As it is, what was done was simply a case of being penny-wise, pound-foolish. We are all apt to make mistakes, and it is unfortunate that the ratepayers should have to pay because the government makes a mistake. But are these settlers to be ruined because the department takes this attitude- "What is that to us? See thou to it."
The government, in fairness and decency to these people ought to see to it that, whether or not the present provision will allow the salmon to go up, these people should not suffer in consequence. They are responsible for what has taken place already- and they should compensate the settlers or accept the offer that has been made them which I submit has been quite reasonable; because where the government speaks of $4,000 this man says he is willing to do a complete job for $S00 or $900. Perhaps a compromise might be decided upon and $750 accepted. The principle that is supposed to animate the ordinary man in dealing with his fellow men should actuate the government in this matter. These people should not be squeezed simply because the government has the whip hand. They can say, "It is just too bad that the best part of the land
belonging to these people, the delta land, which is very valuable in that neighbourhood, should be ruined; but what is that to us?" These people, I would point out to the minister, cannot afford to go to the exchequer court, so that if the government does not compensate them they are simply out of luck. So far as the minister's personal record is concerned, he is entirely in the clear, because the responsibility is not his. This is something that happened before his time. Nevertheless I submit these considerations to him and I hope that he will carefully weigh them. I wish to thank the committee for giving me the opportunity to bring the matter to the minister's attention.

So far as this ladder to which my hon. friend has referred is concerned, it is true that three ladders were built at different times but the work did not give the results which our engineers hoped it would. Recently however, at the request of the member for Comox-Alberni and of others as well, I sent the chief engineer to the district and he made an extensive and complete inquiry into the matter and returned on July 18 with a temporary report, He is advising the building of a fish pass on the side of the dam which will cost about $10,000, and we are accepting the suggestion.

You are going to build the
pass in the rock.
Yes. We are going to incur an expenditure of $10,000 in an effort to rehabilitate the fish run to the Comox watershed.	[DOT]
Thank you.

As to Rosewall creek, some of the letters which my hon. friend has read would not be very good if produced in court in any claim of this kind against the government because this creek runs through the mountains. Part of this territory has been deprived of timber and1 the water runs off very fast, carrying a good deal of gravel and silt down the river. It carries a certain number of logs and a.t times we have to clear the logs. Up to the present, unfortunately, the engineers have reported to the department that the damage to the land is not due to the fact that we cleared logs from the river. It has resulted from the fact that freshets bring down silt and gravel which has accumulated in one place so that to-day the water has to go under the gravel for a distance of about a mile. At all events the report of my engineers is not a complete report. All we could do would
Supply-Fisheries

be to contribute a reasonable amount for the rehabilitation of the creek as far as the fisheries are concerned. We would be abusing our right if we should pay for any damage resulting from the gravel that has been brought down by the freshets. I am quite sure if the hon. member went to the provincial government, under whose jurisdiction this matter comes, he would be able to get something, not for the rehabilitation of the creek in regard to the run of fish but in regard to seeing that in future these freshets do not deposit so much gravel on the borders of this creek.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with keen interest to the remarks of the minister with respect to these two subjects, namely the Puntledge river fish ladder, and the condition at Rosewall creek.
I wish to thank the minister most sincerely for the attitude he has taken with respect to the Puntledge river fish ladder. I was particularly glad to hear him say that the ladder would be cut out of rock at the end of the dam, instead of being stuck up against the dam itself, where it would be just an invitation to be washed out. Cutting it in its proper place, out of the rock at the end, will ensure its permanence, and there will be no more trouble about it going out again. In gratitude for the minister's action I would use my best endeavours to see that it is locally known as the Bertrand fish ladder, and that it be made a permanent tribute to the manner in which he has dealt with the matter, using businesslike and common-sense judgment, and thereby ending a twenty-five-year dispute, through taking action which will lead to the permanent benefit of the fishing industry-an important one in that part of the country. Not only will it benefit the commercial industry, but, as I stated previously, it will add to the sport fishing; because this ladder will also be of advantage to those who indulge in sport fishing.
To come to the other matter of Rosewall creek, I must say that the minister's attitude in this connection is less favourable. No doubt he takes the attitude presented to him by his officials, that the whole trouble is the result of erosion by nature, and so on. But if I did not do it sufficiently before, I should like to emphasize now that is not so. True, the initial trouble began with an act of nature. Logs jammed, and debris caught in a narrow passage and formed what is known as a log

jam. But the point I wish to emphasize to the minister is that it was a jam which was contained, as one might say, between two steep walls. There was a wall of earth or rock on both sides, to quite a considerable height. Consequently that jammed with logs. It did not do any harm, except that it prevented fish from getting through, and in time would have done damage upstream. But it would not do any harm down below where later the ground was flooded. It was partly cutting that jam out that made all the trouble.
The first government officials-and probably I would have done the same thing-did the work in the easiest way. They cut a narrow channel through the logs jammed. Whether they did it in the middle or at the side does not matter. But the result was that while they let the fish up, the logs jammed in such a position that the next freshet which came down turned it around and floated it, not in a narrow passage, not in a gully, but on to a wide flat, where there was nothing to restrain it on either side. It grounded on a gravel bar and stayed there. The gravel silted up behind it, with logs and debris and sand and gravel, and it was that that caused the trouble. I wish to start from that premise, and make it clear that that was the original source of the trouble. Had it been left alone, the flooding of these people's grounds would not have happened, because whatever further damming up might have occurred would have been on the upper side of the log jam.
Now the minister says that I should approach the provincial government and see if they would not undertake to remove this gravel. There are three good reasons against that. The first is that the province is not responsible. The second is that the provincial government knows it is not responsible, and the third is that I have already tried to do that and failed. I have tried, as I say, to get them to take action, but they know the law just as well as I do.
It is not the responsibility of the province. The province will take no responsibility, even for erosion. If a river comes down, eats into a bank, and part of a man's farm falls into the river, they will not take the responsibility. That is the law. But if the action of the river threatens to endanger a road or a bridge, the province will then take the necessary steps. There is of course what the lawyers would call the common law which prevails, that if you take a certain action you are responsible for any damage arising from that action. The province very clearly states that as the dominion caused the trouble by taking away a

Supply-Fisheries
piece of this log jam, instead of taking it all, it is up to the dominion government to take the necessary remedial steps.
If the minister would use his influence with the Minister of Justice to relieve me of responsibility I would feel willing to go into it, after my enforced retirement from the house, and take this man's case up to the exchequer court. But the law of champerty interferes with that.
I can just visualize what will happen. There are thirty-six acres involved. The thirty-six acres are not gone yet, but six acres are gone. The obvious result would be thirty-six acres at $300 an acre-$10,800, or about $11,000, for good will. Would it not be better for the dominion, even from a mercenary viewpoint, let alone the interests of justice and fair play to pay this man, if he is willing to take $750? He will put it into a condition that will satisfy him, and relieve the government of any responsibility further in the matter. Would it not be better to do that than to drag along the weary course of an exchequer court action, and probably get soaked for $10,000 or $11,000? -because the evidence is conclusive. I will not say it is damning, but it is final and conclusive, as disclosed1 by the information I have here. Even the government's own officials have admitted that they have done this, and they have admitted that the results are so-and-so. And these are admissions made by officials of his opponent, so to speak.
Scripture says, Agree with thine adversary quickly while he is in the way lest he turn and rend thee? Would it not be better to give these people this meagre portion of their rights, or remove the trouble, than that the department should get stuck with litigation and perhaps have a $10,000 verdict rendered? I do not appeal to the minister in that form, because I think he is a man who would rise superior to doing things in the cheapest way. That might appeal to some of his officials. I appeal rather to the minister's sense of fair play, which I have seen exercised in several instances since he has held office in his department.
The government is morally1-I think legally, but we will drop that-the government is morally responsible for the damage. It is a continuing damage which will go on and on until the whole of this flat land disappears. I submit it will be only fair and just either to do the work themselves, or to accept the offer this man makes. I cannot do more than I have done to appeal to the minister along these lines. I do hope he will take that sort of view I would expect fom a man who has shown his ability and fair-mindedness in the office he has occupied.

I believe I said everything I have to say before the hon. member spoke. As I told my hon. friend a few minutes ago, the chief engineer is just back from the west after making a study of this question as well as other matters. I have not seen him as yet. He had to go down east, he went out west, he came back here and now he is away for a few days. I will see him and get a verbal report, and if there is anything we can do legally or equitably it will be done.

When the fisheries estimates were last before the committee the discussion centred more upon the fisheries in the mari-times than upon those on the Pacific coast, but this afternoon we are dealing with the Pacific coast fisheries. As the minister knows, but as perhaps many hon. members are not aware, fishing conditions on the Pacific coast are quite different to those in the maritimes. I have one or two matters I should1 like to bring up, although I do not know whether they come under this item 73 dealing with fish culture.
I refer first of all to the depleted condition of the cod fishing grounds on the Pacific coast. I have before me an article which appeared in the Commercial Fisherman's Weekly and which perhaps explains the matter much better than I could do it. This article reports an interview with Clarence L. Musclow, a cod fisherman of fifteen years' standing. I quote:
"The fishery in the lower gulf is all but ruined," Musclow, in Vancouver last week preparing for his sixteenth cod fishing season, stated. "Even on the grounds which have not been fished by the regular cod fishermen, stocks are killed off. Places which in earlier days were good for 2-3,000 pounds of cod, now yield nothing. Excellent fishing locations adjacent to tile international boundary produce only one-half of the quantity taken formerly.
"Even the outside grounds, as off the Vancouver island west coast, are depleted," Musclow continued. "At Swiftsure, fishermen were once knee-deep in lingcod and moved off to get rid of them. The same story is heard closer inshore."
Fishing practices in the past are largely blamed by Musclow for the present condition whilst at the same time he deplores the lack of scientific facts concerning the cod fishery and the slowness of current investigations.
He goes on at considerable length, but I shall not take up the time of the committee to read the entire article. I believe the statements which he makes should be considered seriously by the minister and his departmental officials. The following article which appeared in the Vancouver Sun may interest hon. members. I shall read only a part, as follows:
Years before the war, the cod fishermen supposedly operated on three cents per pound. The
Supply-Fisheries

Japs virtually controlled the cod fishing industry, and 90 per cent of their membership lived on rice, fish, seaweed and Jap sauce, and assiduously sent their money back to their homeland to help build the military and naval equipment that raided Pearl Harbor, Singapore, et cetera.
When these proteges of the three cents per pound fishing operatives were liquidated from the industry a few years ago and the Canadian fishermen finally inherited their own fishing grounds, they found the local codfish grounds 75 to 90 per cent depleted. Whereas the Jap could go out and catch from 500 to 1,500 pounds of cod in a day, the cod fisherman is lucky now to average 100 to 150 pounds per day.
I can vouch for those statements, because I remember when many years ago I first went to live on the gulf islands between Victoria and Vancouver anyone could go into any of the bays and get sufficient cod for the needs of his entire family. It was not long before the Japanese started fishing in those bays, and within three years there was not a cod fish left. They fished day and night until the cod fisheries were entirely ruined. The complaint is being brought up to date by this article which appeared under the name of Musclow. Because of this article and other representations which have been made to me I bring the matter to the attention of the minister and ask him to have a complete investigation made into the depletion of the cod fisheries on the Pacific coast.

For the last several years the fisheries research board has been making an extensive study of the lingcod question and they are still proceeding with their investigations. Just recently the regulations were changed in connection with the lingcod. First, we stipulated a minimum size. Second, we prohibited the use of trawl nets in certain areas where the lingcod seems to be scarce. Third, we are stopping the issue of licences for sunken nets to catch dogfish because while they catch dogfish they also catch quite a lot of lingcod. The cod is one of the most edible fishes we have on the west coast and we hope to be able to reestablish these fisheries as they were before depletion.

On September 11, 1942, the government passed an order in council providing that finnan haddie will mean a combination of smoked haddock, smoked cod, smoked hake and smoked pollock. This was to amend the regulations dealing with canned fish. It reminds me of the man who advertised, I think it was in Paris, that he had for sale a combination of horse and rabbit. When he was asked what that indicated, whether it was fifty per cent horse and fifty per cent rabbit he said, "Yes, it is made up of one

horse and one rabbit." Smoked finnan haddie has been known throughout the world for as far back as we can remember, and it has a
certain reputation of its own. I am speaking only of the canned product, not what is sold in the salted form. That is another story by itself, which I will not go into. I wrote to the government protesting about this matter. I would not have brought this up now because I got my answer and I did not see what more could be done about it. However, since then the trade discovered that my protest was absolutely justified.
My protest was that it was not reasonable or fair, either to the consumer, to the fisherman or to the in-between man, to say that smoked finnan haddie meant something different from what the name implied. The government was saying that it could be smoked cod, smoked hake and smoked pollock. As a rule those fish are inferior to the well known finnan haddie. I asked the government about it and the answer I got was along these lines, that the Meat and Canned Foods Act governs the labelling of canned fish and requires that a true and correct description of the contents of the cans be shown on the labels. It goes on to say:
In view of representations that the pack of canned "finnan haddies" could be considerably increased to -meet the existing demand if permission were granted to include smoked haddock, smoked cod, smoked hake and smoked pollock in the canned product known as "finnan haddies", approval was secured for the definition referred to in order in council P.C. 8167.
So that when the housewife goes to buj' what she thinks is finnan haddie and used to have confidence that she was getting smoked haddie, she may be getting smoked pollock, or ninety per cent, or eighty per cent,, or thirty per cent smoked pollock, or a combination of smoked pollock, smoked cod, smoked hake and these other fish. Smoked pollock is an inferior fish. I forsaw the result and it has come to pass. The general public thought that they were being fooled. They would go to the store and buy what they thought was smoked finnan haddie and find when they opened the can that it was eighty per cent hake or pollock, and they would not go back and buy any more. Naturally it has hurt the popular demand, because once people are deceived they will not buy again. Pork and beans is a well-known product, but if -you put out tins marked "pork and beans" and they contained beef and carrots, where would the demand for pork and beans be? There are people who like pork and beans, but when they buy what they think is pork and beans and find that the can contains other things than pork and beans, the demand drops off.

Supply-Fisheries
That is what has happened with finnan haddie. The demand for it by those who like to eat finnan haddie has dropped off. Some people call this combination which they bought, thinking it was finnan haddie, "cat food." It is an insult to the Scotch origin of finnan haddie to suggest that anything connected with finnan haddie is cat food. The result will be that after the war the demand for canned finnan haddie will drop off.
I cannot understand why a government which says that the Meat and Canned Foods Act requires that a true and correct description of the contents of the cans be shown on the labels allows this to be done. Is the description on the can a true and correct description? No, it is not. When you buy canned finnan haddie nowadays you are buying a sort of grab bag proposition. You may get what you think you are getting, and you may not. You may be getting some inferior fish, less or more of it, as the case may be. I suggest that the minister should look into this and see if it is not too late to put the thing back in its original form. If people want to buy smoked pollock, by all means let them do it, but do not allow smoked pollock to be called something else. Do not let people call a horse a rabbit when it is not.
I was so hopeless of getting any action when I first took this up that I dropped the matter, but I have heard through business channels the demand for so-called finnan haddie is dropping. I wish the minister would give the committee the assurance that he would look into this matter. He does not need to take my word; let him go to those who are engaged in the business. The housewife thinks she is getting canned finnan haddie, and when she finds that it is not finnan haddie at all but smoked pollock or smoked hake or a combination of these other fishes, she feeds it to the cat. The cat may also get fussy after a while and it too may object.

The minister may remember that a great many fishing vessels were taken out of the fishing industry in British Columbia by the military authorities, army, navy or air. Complaint has been made about the depletion of the fishing fleet in many districts. How many boats have b'een returned to the industry in the last year or two, and how many new ones have been built?

There have been about fifty boats returned, some of them very recently.
As to haddie, chicken haddie is a trade name which is used to represent flaked fish. I may say that we are allowing what the hon. member for Comox-Alberni calls cat food to be
called chicken haddie at the request of the trade. I understand that they are pleased with their new product and that it is selling very well. If we ever learned that it was hurting the trade, we would repeal the order, but the information we have up to now is in favour of keeping this product on the market.

I was afraid that the minister would take that up wrongly. I was not talking about chicken haddie at all. Chicken haddie, as the minister says, is a trade name. I wrote to the minister some time ago and I see that I said in my letter:
Chicken haddie means canned haddock or cod or hake or cusk, or any combination of the above.
Chicken haddie is an entirely different product. I was not talking about chicken haddie at all to-day. Chicken haddie is a trade name, just like chicken halibut is. Chicken halibut means halibut, not of an inferior grade, but below a certain size. Inasmuch as it is a trade name, you cannot take any exception to it. If a firm adopts a trade name you know what you are buying, and you get the thing described on the can. But this is a different order in council passed at a different time. It says:
"Finnan haddies"-
Not chicken haddies.
"Finnan haddies" means a combination of smoked haddock, smoked cod, smoked hake and smoked pollock.
The contents are not the same at all because chicken haddie means a combination of haddock, cod and hake, or cusk. I do not know just what cusk is. I was not quarrelling over chicken haddie at all because that is a trade name and you know exactly what you are buying. But when you buy what is supposed to be canned finnan haddie you are getting something that is not finnan haddie. It is a deception of the public and ultimately will be ruinous to the trade because people will discover that they are being deceived and will not buy it again. It is unloading something on the purchaser which is not what it pretends to be. It may be all pollock, or haddock, or hake, or a combination of them. There is no guarantee as to what percentage of finnan haddie you will get, and it will ruin the trade eventually for canned finnan haddie.

Item agreed to.
75. Fisheries Research Board of Canada, $289,000.

I want to compliment the minister on his administration ol the fisheries on the Pacific coast. I should like to ask to what extent the salmon fisheries
Supply-Fisheries

in the Skeena and around the Queen Charlotte islands have been reestablished. I know that the department did some research there last year. What have been the results?

The increase this year, as hon. members may see, is $42,000. The break-up of this amount is as follows: $25,000 for the Skeena river sockeye salmon investigation. The research board is making an investigation in the Skeena river and tributaries, and the biologists with the party are now at these waters studying the reason why there is such a depletion of sock-eye. We hope to be able to restore the sockeye catch to what it was previously. I am told by the scientists that the reduction may be due partly to the great number of rainbow trout in the lakes. Last summer a party went to Babine lake to examine the situation and caught a number of rainbow trout, They ran up to fifteen pounds apiece, and quite a number of small salmon, running up to fifty, were found in the stomachs of every one of them. As the numbers of these trout have increased greatly in recent years it may be necessary to have some of them removed, but the report has not yet reached my department. The fisheries research board is studying very seriously the question, and we hope to be able to restore the sockeye fisheries of the Skeena river.
We are spending $10,000 on the prairie provinces fisheries investigation. An investigation is going on concerning the tullibee and the whitefish. We have in mind the establishment of a biological station for the prairie provinces. A chief biologist has been appointed; his name is Doctor Doan; and two parties are at these waters to-day studying the question.
There are a certain number of problems which are very difficult to handle, but we hope very much to be able to give great assistance to the fishermen in regard to these valuable fisheries. I would not like to say too much on this matter because it might not be good for the trade.
We are to spend $3,000 more on the investigation of the Irish Moss gel and carry on additional scallop, crab and lobster investigation; and $2,000 on the development of new inspection methods and fish plant sanitation; and $2,000 to provide for annual increases.
Can the minister state whether any investigation is being made concerning the pink salmon?

I am informed that, though no investigation is going on now, for ten years there has been an investigation

concerning the pink salmon. We have had reports following these investigations but we have been unable to find any easy way whereby the supply of fish can be restored when it is depleted. It is a big job, not similar to an agricultural problem. Sometimes it takes years of research before it is possible to find the reason why fish are taking to some other areas.

I should like to add my word to that of the hon. member for Skeena regarding the need for further investigations as to pink salmon. I was wondering whether the fisheries research board has ever come to a final conclusion regarding any of their investigations. A large sum of money is voted by parliament every year, but very little interest is taken in the house in what is being done by them. I know that there has been some investigation with regard to the pink salmon. The fact of the matter is that the runs of pink salmon are growing less and are getting to a low level alarming to the fishermen. The fisheries research board has made investigation in regard to this one variety, but have they eome to any final conclusion or made any definite recommendations? I should also like to know whether they have come to any conclusion on any of the investigations which they have made on other varieties of salmon or fish.

The trouble is that the pink salmon is a run that occurs every other year in the Queen Charlotte islands. One year they are plentiful, the next year they are not. We have gathered a certain amount of data which is valuable, but we have not been able as yet to restore the odd year deficiency, and we cannot say that a definite conclusion has been arrived at, because we do not know and we have found as yet no reasons why they do not come in the odd years.

Have they made any investigation about the dogfish carcasses? It has got to a point on the Pacific coast that hundreds of tons of dogfish are being dumped without anything being done with the carcasses. They take the livers out of dogfish for vitamins. Somewhere around three hundred boats, mostly from the United States, are fishing off the west coast of Vancouver Island, and so great has the menace become by the dumping of hundreds of tons of dogfish carcasses on the beaches that the fisheries are being ruined. Have the fisheries research board or the department looked into this matter? It has alarmed the fishermen out there. One writer says:

Supply-Fisherie*
At a time when federal authorities have asked every Canadian citizen to do his utmost to conserve all fats and oils; when the nation's increased meat and poultry supply programme has been endangered through mineral and protein supplement shortage, the loss of millions of pounds of fish meal by throwing overboard dogfish carcasses from which the livers only have been taken, is inexcusable.
Canadian fishermen and reduction plant men are incensed over the great loss. They reckon that in 1943 almost thirty-six million pounds of dogfish went to sea bottom or were dumped on the beaches. It is true that this fish is not eaten by human beings in this country, but surely some value can be found for it, and I have been wondering whether any investigation has been made by the fisheries research board as to the real value of the dogfish.

I should like to say a word on that. I can recall, and no doubt the hon. member for New Westminster can too, when dogfish were the most unpopular things in God's world; anything that could be done to get rid of them was welcomed, because they are horribly destructive of nets, they go through the salmon nets and they will eat salmon too. But suddenly it was discovered during the war that their livers had a value for their oil content, and as the hon. member says there has been a large development of that trade. I am afraid the condition of which he complains is one of those things which cannot be helped. He talks of the carcasses being dumped on the beaches. I would imagine that that would be due, not to their being dumped there but to their having come ashore there, because a man goes out fishing in a comparatively small boat, and when he catches a dogfish he cuts the liver out of it and puts it in a tin and throws the carcass over then and there, and probably it would be eaten by other dogfish, because they are cannibals. But the carcasses which the hon. member says are found on the beaches presumably float there. The fishermen's boats hold only two or three tons each, and to take two or three tons of dogfish to the beach and cut them open there would be a waste of time and space. What they do is cut the liver out then and there when the dogfish is caught. It has been suggested that instead of doing so they should be compelled to take every carcass home. The result would be that the amount of dogfish one man could catch in a day would probably be limited to a ton and a half to two tons, and he would have to go quite a long way to a reduction plant which would take the carcasses, and all the fisherman would get would be three or
four dollars a ton. In the old days when times were bad they used to catch them-I know the Japs did-and sell them to the reduction plants in the winter time. But it was very arduous work and they got only a small wage. They were glad to abandon that work because it proved more profitable to take out the livers, the flesh not being worth anything.
It can be readily understood, of course, that fish that feed on dead bodies would not be palatable, so that flesh would have no market value except for fish meal. Nowadays we have developed a system of catching pilchards, which come in great numbers and which can be more readily, and I might add, more agreeably caught, since it does not involve the same hardships. They are taken to the reduction plants. So that the demand for dogfish would be small indeed and it would not pay to catch them, and the regulation would be most prohibitive if they were compelled to take the carcasses in because the only place where they could be sold would be at reduction plants scattered far and wide, so that they might have to go a hundred miles and more to get to a plant. It would not pay them. It would kill the industry. The liver contents are badly needed, but nothing can be done in the meantime. I think there would be a greater gain from the money obtained from the liver as against the loss of the body, which is of no edible value.

There is another aspect of the matter I overlooked. On the one hand you have five or six million pounds of fish meat, and on the other you have five or six million pounds of dead fish which,, the fishermen say, destroys the fishing ground. It is said on good authority that within two hours of the dogfish carcasses being dumped into a bay, the live dogfish and the cod leave the bay entirely. That is something for the fisheries research board to look into. They might ascertain whether the dumping of dogfish into a bay does result in driving out from the fishing beds the other dogfish and codfish.

I congratulate the ministry of fisheries on its intention to set up a research station in Manitoba. This will greatly benefit the northern lakes of that province. The minister knows quite well the difficulties we have had there, catching fish and sending them to the United States boundary only to find that the fish were not acceptable there, so that they became a dead loss. I am quite sure that the establishment of this research station will overcome that difficulty and will get to the bottom of the grievance that exists in the northern lakes. I think the minister
Supply-Fisheries

knows what I am referring to, and I do not wish to give it more publicity than is necessary. I would point out to him an ideal situation for this research station. At the mouth of the Red river there is the town of Selkirk, which is an ideal station, because we have cheap electric power, a great deal of water and accommodation for employees that are likely to be engaged there, and it is adjacent to the capital of Manitoba. There is good service by bus and there is a good pavement. There are quite a few fish-packing concerns there which could work in with a research station.
