There is a persistent
rumour that Atlantic salmon are being planted in the tributary waters of lake Ontario and in the upper regions of the St. Lawrence. Is that simply a rumour or is there truth in it?

First, in reply to the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), I may say that we have not decided yet where the biological station will be, but we are looking into all these matters and the station will certainly be placed advantageously as recommended. I understand that it is important that the processors, the fishermen and the fish should be able to meet at the same place for the purposes of the biological station.
As regards the question asked by the hon. member for Leeds, the department has nothing to do with the planting of salmon in lake Ontario. I know that one of the provinces, I am not sure whether Ontario or Quebec, has had articles in the newspapers to the effect that they would try to plant Atlantic salmon along the St. Lawrence. Years ago salmon were plentiful in most of the rivers tributary to the St. Lawrence up to Lachine rapids, but to-day they have disappeared. I know it is being done, but not by my department.
[Mr. Bryce.1
Has the department any publications on research that has been done into fish diseases in the northern lakes and the great lakes?

We have a private report, from Doctor Miller which is quite interesting. It is a scientific report, but we do not intend to publish it. It deals with fish diseases. If the hon. member wishes to see it 1 shall be pleased to show it to him.
Are they continuing this work and trying to remedy the situation?

Yes. They are continuing the work and we are sure to make some progress, if not improving the situation at least in regulating the trade so that the commodity will be acceptable to importing countries.

I support what the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) has said. I presume he is referring, when he mentions the northern lakes, to lake Athabasca and Great Slave lake. I brought up this question a few years ago-
Last year.

Perhaps it was before tlr minister's time. I had just been up there and learned about that skin disease, and the minister at that time assured me that it would be cleared up promptly. Has it been cleared up?

I remember
that last year the hon. gentleman drew my attention and that of the committee to Great Slave lake and1 lake Athabaska. We have a party at work there now, a biologist and three or four men, who went out two or three months ago and are in the field now. I do not think anything can be done commercially at least during this year, or until the end of the war, but a>t least we have a biologist there studying the question.

Item agreed to.
77. To provide for Canadian share of expenses of the international Pacific salmon -fisheries commission under treaty between Canada and the United States for the protection, preservation and extension of the sockeye salmon fisheries of the Fraser river system, $42,000.

There is one matter I should like to place before the minister, which is dealt with in a resolution passed at a meeting held in Victoria this year. Perhaps I cannot do better than read the resolution itself:
At its meeting held in the city of Tacoma, Washington, in April, 1944, the Pacific Northwest Trade Association requested the governments of Canada and the United States to give

Supply-Fisheries
immediate attention to the adequate protection of the Pacific coast fisheries of the two nations. These nations have spent many millions of dollars, have imposed many restrictions on their fishermen and fishing vessels, and have created two international commissions to preserve and develop these coastal fisheries, yet much of this expenditure will have been wasted and much of the effort lost unless these fisheries are protected for an adequate distance off-shore against the encroachments of Japanese or nationals of other countries than the United States or Canada.
Now, therefore, be it resolved: That this association now meeting at Victoria, British Columbia, this June 27, 1944, again calls the matter to the attention of the two governments, again points out the necessity for prompt and effective action being taken, and urges that the consideration of this important Pacific coast problem shall not be confused with the divergent problems of the Atlantic, or any other region, but be dealt with as a separate and distinct problem which can and should be considered upon its own merits, and at once.
Who is asking that?

The Pacific northwest trade association.
The Fraser river basin is one of the most valuable fishery spawning regions in the world, and is frequented by all varieties of Pacific coast salmon as well as by other species of fish, yet in the creation of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission, by treaty between Canada and the United States, the powers of that commission were confined to dealing with sockeye salmon alone.
For the information of hon. members may I say that five varieties of salmon frequent the waters of British Columbia, and of these varieties only one, namely, sockeye, is under the jurisdiction of this international commission. In this resolution this association asks that all varieties come under its control for investigation, research, protection and rehabilitation.
Now therefore, be it resolved: That the governments of the two nations be urged to amend the treaty referred to so that the commission created thereby shall be authorized to deal with all varieties of salmon, and any other valuable commercial fish which are found in the Fraser river basin.
Too often in the past hydro electric, irrigation and other construction projects have been planned without consideration having been given to their effect on important fishery resources, although in many instances, it would have been possible that had such considerations been given the one might have been developed without harm to the other, and although, in some instances at least, it was doubtful whether the project was of greater economic value to the public at large than the fishery.
Now, therefore, be it resolved: That before any hydro electric, irrigation or other construction project be authorized which may seriously affect any substantial fishery, either recreational or commercial, a careful survey should be made by some disinterested public agency to determine the actual and relative values of such project, and such fishery and that every endeavour be made not to sacrifice
the one for the other, or, in any way, to prejudice the general public interest.
Be it further resolved: That before any hydro electric, irrigation or other construction project which affects an existing fishery be authorized, it should also be mandatory that the provincial or the state or other government having jurisdiction over such projects notify its respective fishery department of such prospective projects in order that adequate investigation of any fishery involved may be made before there is any commitment, direct or indirect, or authorization of such projects.
May I interrupt for a moment to say that we expect that hydro-electric development on the Fraser river to take place in the future. The whole British Coumbia watershed has been surveyed and mapped out with that purpose in mind. The fisheries commission do not take the stand that there shall not be any hydro electric development. They do say, however, that before any such hydro development is proceeded with or any dams constructed, consideration should be given to the possible effect of such development on, the fisheries. Mention has been made from time to time of the fishways which have been built in the great dams on the Columbia river, some of them costing as much as seven or eight million dollars. Hon. members may be interested to know that although these fishways are presumably successful, the fact is that the Columbia river fisheries are going down- year by year, and I believe independent observers would say that in time the construction of these dams across that river may mean the destruction of those fisheries.
Do the fish keep going up the fishways?

Yes, they do, but the young fry have to be brought down again, and that has not been entirely successful. The fish can go up above the dams and spawn, but the young fry coming down again have met with difficulties. So that year after year those fisheries have been going down, and competent observers say that if some further steps are not taken the fisheries of the Columbia river may be completely destroyed. That is the reason for the warning coming from this association, that when hydTO-eleetric development on the Fraser river or its tributaries is under consideration, care be taken to see that the same thing does not happen there. We are not taking the stand that there shall not be any hydro-electric development, because we realize that as the population of the province increases there will have to be some development along these lines.	.
Mr. O'NEILL: I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for New Westminster, who apparently has approached this

Supply-Fisheries

question pretty much from the sole point of view of the fishermen, who say nothing must be done that will destroy the salmon fisheries. But there are other people in the province of British Columbia who are just as anxious to see that we do not make the whole interior of the province and all the tributaries of the Fraser river a spawning ground for salmon. For many years the people of Kamloops have looked forward to the day when power would be developed on the Adams river, which is one of the tributaries of the Thompson, which in turn is one of the tributaries of the Fraser, and so undoubtedly will be considered one of those streams upon which hydro-electric power must not be developed if such development would by any chance interfere wfith the salmon fisheries. While I am in sympathy with the demand of the fishermen that their fishing grounds should not be destroyed, on the other hand it does seem to me, to use a railway phrase, that we have been asleep at the switch in this country. We have permitted our great neighbours to the south to erect barriers on their rivers in order to develop power, and practically to destroy the salmon fisheries of the Columbia river; and now, to make sure these salmon fisheries are maintained as much as possible, you are going to make the interior of British Columbia a spawning ground for salmon for the benefit of the fishermen of the Fraser river and also the fishermen of the United States. It does seem to me that the farmers, and those now living in the interior of British Columbia, who have waited for years and years for power developments, are now to be denied the benefits of that electrical power on their farms because it may interfere with the salmon fisheries.
There are a lot of things to be taken into consideration besides fisheries. If provision can be made under which these tributaries may still be used as spawning grounds for salmon, without interfering with hvdro-electric development, then I would be quite prepared to discuss the question. But if it must be discussed from the point of view that it shall not interfere with salmon fisheries, then I am not prepared to discuss it at all. If it can be considered from the other point of view of developing power on these rivers without unduly restricting the salmon spawning grounds, all well and good. But I suggest to the Minister of Fisheries that when this question is being discussed the rights of other people, besides salmon fishermen, must be given some consideration.

I do not know if the hon. member for Kamloops heard clearly the remarks I made. I was careful to point out that the Pacific salmon fisheries commission tMr. O'Neill.]
realized fully that there had to be hydroelectric power development. If the hon. member was paying any attention to the resolution I read he would know that very point was emphasized by me. I am not altogether surprised by the hon. member's remarks, because only a week or so ago a debate took place in his city in regard to an old dam which was constructed long years ago by a logging company. That dam is at the entrance to a lake known as Adams lake. It has been in disrepair for I do not know how many years. For the past twenty years it has not been used by the logging company. When it was built and operated by the logging company there was a fishway through it, into Adams lake-which, by the way is a lake with at least eighty miles of spawning grounds available. No great difficulty was experienced in those years by the fish. The logging company, however, has now been carrying out its operations by truck. Over the course of years the dam has fallen into disrepair, and for many years salmon coming to spawn there have been unable to get past. So that the fisheries commission in its investigations, after looking over the matter, sought the removal of this dam. They were not seeking the removal of hydro-electric development. Rather they were asking for the removal of a dam which had not been used for twenty yeass and which was a menace to the salmon going to (he lake. Those are the facts of the case.
As I said, there must be development of hydro-electric power in British Columbia, and there must also be development of our fisheries. The two must go hand in hand. My warning to the government and the country is that from a fisheries point of view we cannot sit idly by and see the power companies erect dams irrespective of whether they kill the fish or not, as happened across the line.

Mr. Chairman, we have heard the view of power versus salmon ably presented by the two hon. members who have just spoken. There is a great deal of truth in both arguments. With reference to the situation in respect to dams, of which the hon. member for New Westminster spoke-a dam which has been a menace to fish for twenty years, and for which no one would admit responsibility-might I say that that could easily have been settled. As a matter of fact we had the same condition in my district. There was no possibility of its being used for power purposes, and it was a menace to salmon coming up. Therefore I gave a good friend of mine five sticks of stumping powder-and that was the end of that; and it saved a lot of trouble.

Supply-Fisheries
If I heard the hon. member for New Westminster correctly, he read a resolution passed by a body with which he is connected stating that these things should be investigated. There is no doubt that they will have to be investigated, having in mind the greatest good to the greatest number. It will be found that in some rivers it will be necessary, and perhaps advisable, to let the fish go and to proceed with the power development. In other cases it might be the other way round- that the power development would not be substantial, and that it would be more valuable as a fishing area. For instance it would be inconceivable to abandon the Fraser or Columbia rivers entirely as sources of fish, because they are perhaps two of the greatest fisheries rivers in the world. It ultimately boils down to this, that the choice must be made as to which it may be advisable to drop. Perhaps it might be wise to keep the power development in certain rivers, or perhaps the tributaries of those rivers, and leave the fish in other rivers-that is, in other cases it would be the other way round.
I wish now to speak about another point to which the hon. member for New Westminster referred, and to which reference was made by the association for which he speaks. While I did not hear him clearly, I did gather he was pointing out that there was some danger of attacks being made upon our fisheries, not in the rivers themselves within our territories, but outside the rivers.
Outside the .three-mile limit?

Yes, outside the three-mile limit. While the condition has not been the same since the war, there wag a pronounced and clear case a few years ago. Fish have peculiar habits. There is not one fish for every square yard or for every ten square yards in the ocean. Fish travel in well-defined movements. Aircraft, looking down, can spot these movements just as they can spot submarines. The conclusion is that they can be seen hundreds of miles off shore. The particular case I have in mind was in connection with the development at Bristol bay, where the Americans get large quantities of fish. It is up in the Alaska area, and the Americans take enormous supplies of fish out of there. Well, it was discovered that our oriental friends, the Japanese, with their usual astuteness, had cleaned out the greater part of their own area-because a Jap's idea of fishing is to take the last fish and the last fin out of an area, whether it is his own or anybody else's. So they go and beg, borrow or steal somebody else's fish. He had depleted his own fisheries and he was then engaged in
100-327i
depleting the fisheries he had leased from the Russians, and saw the possibilities in the excellent waters of Bristol bay.
It is generally recognized-I do not know as to whether there is any international law on the point-that the territorial waters or rights of a nation shall extend three miles beyond its coastline. And I believe it is further recognized that that distance shall be computed from the headlands-that is, one would not compute it from a deep bay, but rather from headland to headland. The Japanese, probably keeping within the law, came up there and ran a big mother ship fol canning salmon. Then they spread a net- I have heard it was 200 miles long; I do not know if that is correct. However it is said they ran an enormous length of net, sufficient to run practically across the mouth of these Alaskan waters. They kept far enough out so that they could not be interfered with under territorial waters regulations, and yet sufficiently close to get the benefit of the fish going into those waters.
If they could do it there, then it would be only a short time before they would do it lower down and cut off our supply going to the Fraser river. The United States made a protest in a friendly way, as one friendly nation to another, stating that the Japanese were not playing the game-even though perhaps they were keeping within their actual rights. After all, these were American fish spawned there, taken care of, and protected. The Americans would not let their white fishermen take these fish, except at certain times, in order to protect them. And it was just a little bit too strong to see the Japanese come along and clean up the whole output. The Japanese replied with their usual courtesy and said that they were sorry but the Americans were mistaken; they were not trying to take salmon, they were simply prospecting for crabs. They had taken out this large ship, equipped it with canning, appliances, and all they were doing was prospecting for crabs. They were so sorry that the Americans, their good friends, would even suspect that they were capable of doing anything	that	might be	considered	an
unfriendly act, the Americans whom they loved so much and continued to love until the last minute before Pearl Harbor.
The Americans were not fooled, and they replied in like manner. They said they accepted the statement and the assurances of the Japanese, they were quite sure they were sincere when they said they were only prospecting for crabs, but unfortunately or fortunately they sent an aeroplane up. It came down low enough to the mother ship that they
Supply-Fisheries

were able to see the names on the cases of salmon that were being packed and it therefore looked as though the Japanese government had been mistaken in saying that they were prospecting only for crabs. The Japanese government then reiterated their assurances of devotion to the United States and so on; they said the Americans must have been mistaken and anyhow they had given orders it was not to be done again.
Of course it was continued. This was just about a year before the war. The United States fishermen got a little tired of using diplomacy and they decided to help themselves. They sent down to Seattle for a couple of hundred rifles and they said that when they got those back they would settle the situation by more drastic and practical means. Then the war broke out and that waa the end of the matter for the time being.
As the hon. member for- New Westminster has pointed out, we should negotiate an agreement with the United States similar to the one in connection with the Columbia river salmon. It could cover not only the sockeye but other varieties of fish. I urge the government to consider seriously this aspect of the matter. There is no doubt that the Japs were legally within their rights. It was suggested about that time that a ship was coming out from Norway for the same purpose. The United States government made friendly representation and the thing was stalled off for the time being. But the question will have to be faced sooner or later. Some people will say that it can be done by having a gentleman's agreement or by some other means to extend the territorial waters of Canada beyond the three-mile limit to what is known as the continental shelf. But there are objections to this method because the continental shelf varies. At some places it is quite close to Canada, and at other places it is a considerable distance away. I do not think the problem can be met in that way. It seems to me that the solution is in having an agreement with the United States -along the lines of the one in connection with salmon. As soon as the war is ended the Japanese will again be in a position to- do this, or it may be the Norwegians or someone else. They will come here and take advantage of the millions of dollars we vote year after year protecting the birth and early life of the salmon. Are we going to sit. down and watch them take these fish by putting down nets beyond the territorial limits?
I do hope the minister will take note of this. This thing needs investigation and it needs foresight. We are on terms of good friendship

with the United States at the moment and now is the time to make an agreement of that kind.
To what extent does this item number 77 duplicate the $1,000,000 item in connection with the fisheries commission?

This item is only for the maintenance of the commission, whereas the other item is a capital expenditure for the building of a fish pass at Hell's Gate and to provide means of overcoming other obstacles.

We are fortunate in having three members from British Columbia who know as much about fishing as any other members in this house. I am not one of them, but Hell's Gate happens to be in my riding. The hon. member for New Westminster, the hon. memebr for Comox-Alberni and the hon. member for Skeena have a thorough knowledge of the fishing industry. I want to say a word about the hon. member for New Westminster. I think he knows more than the other two hon. members because he comes from a riding which is next to mine. As Hell's Gate is in my riding I am much interested in this matter. I want to pay my tribute to the hon. member for New Westminster, and when I do that I think I speak for the fishermen of British Columbia, certainly for those in my riding. The work carried on by this commission, of which he is a member, has done considerable for the fishing industry of British Columbia.
A short time ago the hon. member for Comox-Alberni referred to the benefits accruing to the country from the fishing industry. If my memory serves me rightly, the value of the fisheries in British Columbia alone in 1941 amounted to $21,000,000. The benefits from that production accrue to the whole dominion.
This commission has done excellent work. I think the principal reason for that is that the two leading technical men in the commission come from my riding. The deputy minister of fisheries does not exactly come from my riding but he showed excellent judgment in marrying a lady from my riding. His chief assistant does come from my riding.
I do not think I have any more to say on this matter except, that I hope there will be no question at all about passing the $1,000,000 vote. This is a small matter when we consider the value of this industry. If I am not mistaken in my figures, on the basis of the prices received last year and the run of 1913,

Supply-Fisheries
the value of this production in British Columbia alone would be 840,000,000. Surely- we can afford to pass this vote.

78. Grant to the united maritime fishermen's association, $3,000.

On June 30 when the minister's estimates were, before the committee he referred to the brief presented by the united maritime fishermen's association, and in referring to it he said, as reported on page 4416 of Hansard:
The brief presented to us by the united fishermen says that they do not want the unrestricted use of trawlers, meaning that they do not want the trawlers to fish anywhere. We are going to see, through the system of granting a licence, that the trawlers fish far away from the shore.
I think the minister has misinterpreted the brief presented by the united maritime fishermen's association. Their brief reads:
Clearly then the unrestricted use of trawlers is inimical to the interest of the inshore fishermen, and on behalf of its members this association must continue its opposition to them.
The unrestricted use to which they refer there is not only the unrestricted use of the fishing grounds but unrestricted use in so far as the number of beam trawlers is concerned. It is important that we be seized of that difference. The reason why the united maritime fishermen are opposed to -the beam trawler is that it affects a large number of fishermen, and an increase in the number of beam trawlers tends to put fishermen out of business and centralize the industry in two or three places in Nova Scotia, Halifax and Lunenburg for example. I hope that the minister will not continue with that interpretation.

It means
both.

If the minister understands that, there is no need for me to pursue the matter further. I agree with the united maritime fishermen; I am opposed to the trawler. I have said a great deal about it before, and I shall not repeat. I have not changed my mind.

79. To provide for transportation, dressing and dyeing other expenses incidental to receiving and disposing of fur seal skins accruing to Canada pursuant to provisional fur seal agreement between Canada and the United States by exchange of notes dated December 8 and 19, 1942, $120,000.

As the minister and perhaps the members of the committee know, a treaty regarding pelagic sealing was made in 1911 between four countries. In 1941 the treaties
were terminated. We are receiving considerable value each year from the United States, and at no expense to us, because under the treaty we prevent our fishermen from interfering with the seals on their way north to the Pribilof islands. Our share last year was twenty per cent of the seals caught, which gave Canada 23,400 skins. These when processed are worth $50 apiece. The processing costs from $12 to $15 apiece, so that Canada got roughly $800,000 as her share. I have a suggestion to make to the minister. I think that he should consider sending a man or men up to the Pribilof islands from Canada for a few days each year, if for nothing else than to show that we are interested in what is being done by the United States in regard to the killing and taking of seals from the Pribilof islands. We have had considerable benefit from the treaty, but I do not think we have had a representative go to the Pribilof islands to keep an eye on what is being done there. Perhaps the minister would give that suggestion his serious consideration.

As the hon. member for New Westminster has said, this is a very valuable asset for Canada. Here is an example of how the fur seal population is being restored through international cooperation. We have a treaty with the United States which has just been renewed. We have no representative in the Pribilof islands. We do not doubt at all the honesty of the United States authorities. They number the barrels containing the skins and we have the privilege of indicating by number which barrels we w'll take. For instance we may say that we will take barrel No. 3, barrel No. 5, barrel No. 13. and so on, so that we have an equal chance of getting representative skins.

What I had in mind was not so much to check up on the United States authorities, because after all they are acting in good faith and we must assume that they are. But when the treaty was first signed, four countries were a party to it, United States, Canada. Russia and Japan. We do not know what countries may want to enter into a treaty _ of this kind after the war. My suggestion is that we should send a representative up there to show our interest in the matter and to gather information so that we shall be better able to discuss the matter when the time comes for renewing the treaty.

I understand that under the original treaty the Russians gave us fifteen per cent, United States fifteen per cent, and the Japanese fifteen per cent of the catch.

On Pribilof island the proportions were as follows: Canada, 15 per cent; United States, 70 per cent; Russia, 0; Japan. 15 per cent. On Commander island: Canada. 15 per cent; United States, 0; Russia, 70 per cent; Japan, 15 per cent. On Robben island. Canada, 10 per cent; United States, 10 p r cent; Russia, 10 per cent; Japan, 70 per cent
Japan repudiated the treaty a year or two ago, did she not?
Yes.
What is the deal now?

The agreement is that the proportion that Japan was taking is divided between Canada and the United^ States. Japan has abrogated the treaty, but of course they are free to catch seals passing around their own territory.
Item agreedi to.
80. To provide for payment of a bounty for the destruction of harbour seals, $15,000.
How much do we pay now for each individual hair seal shot, and how much was paid out of this vote last year?
We pay S2.50 per nose. The nose is the proof which the fisherman supplies. Last year we paid out $6,245.

I would suggest that the
amount paid per seal is not enough. That is illustrated by the fact that you have so much money left out of last years' vote. If you -paid out only $6,000 odd, it shows that the fishermen are nob much interested. A hair seal when shot immediately sinks, so even if the fisherman shoots one his chance of recovering it is small. You may shoot half a dozen and recover only one. These hair seals can do great damage to a fisherman's nets, and a fisherman with a long line of nets out cannot afford to leave his fishing when he is perhaps getting a good run of fish to shoot a hair seal for $2.50. The greatest destruction of the seals in years gone by was through the government patrol boats on the Pacific, which supervise the enforcement of the law. At certain seasons of the year the boats would go to the breeding grounds and shoot or club the seals and much greater destruction was done in that way than by casual shooting by individual fishermen. You can hardly expect a fisherman to drop his fishing when he is having a nice run of fish to go after one seal. That we are not paying enough is indicated by the
IMr. Neill.1
fact that only $6,000 was paid out of the vote last year. I suggest that the amount paid per seal should- be raised to $5 and- that as soon as the war is over aggressive steps should be taken to renew the destruction done by these patrol boats. During the war these patrol boats have been taken over for other purposes or have been continuing their activities in a very limited fashion. They have not been able to do the destruction on the breeding grounds which they did before. I hope the government will provide the money. It is not very much; in fact it is not enough. The bounty should be increased in order to encourage people to go after these hair seals; also they should try to strengthen the service of fisheries patrol boats so that their activities will be renewed when the war is over. We pay to catch wild animals in British Columbia, such as the cougar and the wolf, a much larger bounty than that. With the aid of a good dog a man can get a cougar comparatively easily, yet the bounty is something like ten or twelve dollars. Two and a half dollars is not enough, when a man can go out and catch dogfish and take out their livers and get far more money that way.

I should like to join my representations with those of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and also to commend -the minister for the steps he has taken so far to help out in the Fraser river. For some unknown reason, during the past two years, the seals have grown to enormous numbers. I myself last year counted on one bar at least a thousand seals, and the closest you can get is about half a mile It may be possible to go to the rookeries and kill these seals, but in th-e Fraser river you cannot get nearer than half a mile to them; one shot from a gun, and instantly they are in the water. The minister has been good enough to interest himself in an endeavour to get rid of them to so-me extent in the Fraser river. The-ir numbers have grown so much that fishermen are refusing to put their nets in -the water. At a meeting I attended during the Easter recess, fishermen said that of every ten salmon in a net, seven would be destroyed before the net could be picked up. due to the seals running along and biting them, and the net would be destroyed as well. I ask the minister seriously to consider the increasing of the -bounty so as to encourage the fishermen to go after them to a greater extent because, as pointed out by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, when a fisherman takes a shot at them and hits a seal, the seal sinks, unless the man is close enough to get it before it goes down too deep,

Supply-Fisheries
and thereby many' fishermen are discouraged from attempting to get these hair seals. They are in the Fraser river by the thousands. I do not know why they stay there. One suggestion is that it is because of the gunnery practice of naval and air forces outside the gulf.
I think the minister should redouble his efforts if he can, and consider increasing the bounty as suggested by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.

The hon. member for New
Westminster talks about numbers of seals as great as one thousand on a sand bar. I had no idea that things were as bad as that. The suggestion was made that they should be mined on these beaches where they go to sun themselves. Has anything been done along that line, and with what results?

Last year we made an extensive study of this problem, and we took some members of the Department of National Defence for Air to view these sand bars and tell us if it would be practicable to install mines there or endeavour to bomb them when they congregated there; but it was too difficult We were told that the weight of these seals is not enough to explode bombs, and that to use them under the circumstances would be very dangerous. Then we got officers of the Department of National Defence for Air to practise shooting at these seals on certain days of the week when the fishermen were not there, and we believe that they have destroyed a certain number; but there were some protests from the neighbours. We are still studying the question. We do not know exactly upon what lines success will lie, but the board is still giving attention to the subject.

Item agreed to.
82. To .provide for the replacement of the Gaspe peninsula fisheries experimental station, $35,000.

The hon. member for Gaspe is not in the chamber at the moment. I believe the member from that district is a soldier and he may be on military duty. I am glad to see that the minister has an estimate to do something to increase Gaspe fisheries. As far as I can see, Gaspe is one of the forgotten areas in Canada.
Mr. BERTRAND (Laurier!: Fisheries administration is under the provincial authorities.
I see you are providing for a vote of $35,000.
I can explain to the hon. member what it is for. .

It is to provide for the replacement of the Gaspe peninsula fisheries experimental station. All I want to say is that I am in accord with this vote, because it is beneficial to Gaspe and will be beneficial to the country. Gaspe was perhaps the first part of Canada which was touched by explorers;
I believe Jacques Cartier landed there in 1534; and to me it is more or less neglected country, but it is very beautiful, and whatever the minister can do to help the Gaspe people he should do. I would not have got up to say anything on this item had the hon. member for Gaspe been here to say it himself.

Item agreed to.
S3. To provide for Canadian share of expenses of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission to overcome obstructions to the ascent of sockeye salmon at Hell's Gate Canyon, and for investigation and overcoming obstructions to such salmon at other points on the Fraser river watershed, $1,000,000.

This sum is for the construction of two passes at Hell's Gate. I just want to say that I hope these passes will be finished by the month of April next, and if we can restore the sockeye run on the Fraser River by the building of these two passes it will be a great thing for the fishermen of British Columbia. Just to give an example, I might say that if in 1941 the catch had been as good as the catch of 1913, the year before the landslide, at the prices of salmon in 1941, instead a return of about $8 million it would have given a return of $40 million. We hope to be able to restore this run on this basis.
I do not want to let this item pass without paying a tribute to the members of the Pacific salmon fisheries commission. They jiave been working for six years, and I want to mention especially my hon. friend the hon. member for New Westminster, who was chairman last year; Mr. Edward W. Allen, barrister of Seattle, who is chairman this year; Mr. B. M. Brennan, Doctor Thompson, Mr. Milo Bell, and others who have worked very hard and given a great deal of their time and gone out of their way for the successful planning of these passes, which investigations now show have certainly been needed for the past thirty years.

On behalf of the members of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission I wish to thank the minister for introducing this vote of $1 million, which will be matched by $1 million from the United
Supply-Fisheries

States. This will take care of the two fish passes, at Hell's Gate canyon and thirty-seven obstructions on the Fraser river estuary. I wish to thank the minister for the vote on ' behalf of the commission of which I am a member.

Item agreed to. .
8Jf. To provide for the extension of educational work in cooperative producing and selling among fishermen, $50,000.
Will the minister indicate how and where this work is being carried on, and the possibility of its being extended to other parts of Canada?

This item of $50,000 is the same as the item that appeared in the supplementaries last year. We are asking for $10,000 more in order to help in some other fields. This is probably the best-spent money in this department, because the work done at St. Francis Xavier, Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere and the university of British Columbia is of immense value. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Under this item there is a matter which I should like to discuss with the minister for a few moments. I have already taken it up with him by correspondence, but unless something has been done about it recently, the request I have in mind has not yet been met. I am speaking on behalf of the women who do the char work in some of the public buildings that are under the Department of Public Works. My knowledge relates particularly to the fedenJ building in the city of Winnipeg and other Li ildings there that come under the direction of this department, The women who do this work feel that they should be entitled to some of the privileges that go with service extending over many years and that the privileges accorded the men doing similar work should be accorded to them. There are two of these privileges in particular about which I wish to speak-holidays with pay and a certain amount of sick leave without loss of pay. Shortly after the matter was brought to my attention last fall I wrote to the minister on October 6, 1943, setting out the situation and asking that be give it his consideration. Anticipating that there might be some argument over the status of these women, whether they were part-time, temporary employees or permanent employees,
I made reference in writing the minister to the 
notice of employment that was given to one of these women in Winnipeg, whom I happen to know, which notice I hold in my hand at the present time. It is on the departmental letterhead.
Department of Public Works, Canada Chief Architects' Branch
Maintenance Office-Dominion Public Buildings
In replying please quote file No. 1177-48.
The letter is dated June 16, 1941, and is addressed to a lady in Winnipeg doing this kind of work. The letter says in part:
This is to advise yon that the hon. the Minister of Public Works has been pleased to appoint you, during pleasure, as a charwoman on the above,-
"The above" refers to P.W.D. Staff, Winnipeg, Manitoba.
-at a remuneration of $660 per annum, for which you will be required to work a minimum of 7 hours per day, your appointment to date from the day on which you commence your duties.
The letter goes on to tell the lady whom she is to get in touch with and sets out certain other particulars in connection with her employment. The point I wish to emphasize is that the appointment was made on the basis of a certain amount per annum; she was not hired at a prevailing hourly rate. It was at an annual salary, if you wish to call it that, of $660. I pointed out when I wrote to the minister on October 6 that further evidence of the annual basis on which these women are employed is found in the fact that if they lose time owing to illness their pay cheques are docked and the amount they are docked varies according to the number of days in the month in which they are absent. In other words, if they lose a day in February they lose more money from their cheque than if they lose a day in December, which I suggest is evidence of the fact that they are paid on an annual basis and not on a daily or an hourly rate. I happen to know that some of these women have been employed with the Department of Public Works doing char work in the public buildings in Winnipeg for as long as ten or fifteen years, so that they can hardly be referred to as temporary employees. The dutirs of these women have been set out in a memorandum which reads:
Charwoman. Definition of class:	Under
supervision, to perform routine cleaning work in a government building as assigned.
Examples:	sweeping and scrubbing floors;
washing windows and woodwork; dusting and cleaning furniture; emptying wastebaskets and spittoons.
Qualifications . . .

Supply-Public Works

Are they under the civil
service?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is a part of the problem.
I am wondering why charwomen should have to go through the civil service.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
To continue, note the requirements these women must meet:
Qualifications: preferably primary school education; knowledge of simple cleaning work and implements; ability to read and write; willingness to work; good physical condition.
Compensation: Prevailing rates shall apply.
I suppose that is probably where the confusion comes in. You have a memorandum on the one hand that says the compensation shall be the prevailing rates, and on the other hand when these women are engaged they are given the kind of notice to which I have already referred which states that they are engaged at a remuneration established on an annual basis. I have before me as well a memorandum setting out the specifications of the work of a cleaner and helper. In this instance the reference is to the men who do work similar to that done by the women. I could read it, but I need hardly take the time. There are a few duties included in the work assigned to men which are not included in the work assigned to women, but the definition of the class is strikingly similar. It reads:
Under supervision, to perform routine cleaning and janitor work as assigned and in some cases to perform or assist in general household or domestic work.
Perhaps I should read the qualifications in
this case as well:
Ability to read and write and preferably primary school education; knowledge of simple cleaning work and implements; willingness to work; good physical condition.
Compensation, annual: $1,020, $1,080, $1,140.
Note: For part-time work the compensation shall be in the same proportion to the above rates as the number of hours worked to standard working hours.
I want to emphasize the fact that there is a striking similarity between the definition of the class under which the men work and the class under which the women work; there are also striking similarities in their duties and qualifications, but the women are treated as though they were temporary, part-time employees whereas the men are treated as permanent employees. Apparently on the basis of that distinction the women are denied holidays with pay and sick leave without loss of pay. Nevertheless, anticipating that argument, as I have already pointed out, I drew to the attention of the minister when I first wrote
him the nature of the document these women receive when they are engaged.
The minister replied to my letter under date of October 26, 1943, and said in part:
The situation is as follows. The char staff work only part of the day. They are paid the
prevailing hourly rate in tire disirict. h * work must be considered as extra; is not hard; and is much in demand in all parts of the country.
That would seem to place a premium on it,
I might interject.
In any part-time prevailing rate work there is a general rule, followed by both industry and government, that holidays and sick leave are not applicable, and this rule has been followed in the particular ease you have reference to in Winnipeg.
We do not consider, particularly under circumstances of to-day, that any change should
be undertaken.
Yours sincerely,
Alphonse Fournier.
Inasmuch as I had gone to the trouble to emphasize the nature of the document which these women receive when they are employed, I felt that I had to reply to the minister's letter and I did so on November 16, calling attention again to the kind of notice these women receive, at least the women in Winnipeg, appointing them on an annual basis. I want to emphasize that there are many women in that city who have been doing this work for a good many years. There is nothing parttime or temporary about it. They have a set number of hours which they work every working day the year round, and as yet they have not been granted these two concessions.
In reply to my letter of November 16 the minister wrote me under date of November 23. This letter was somewhat shorter but slightly more welcome. He said:
Dear Mr. Knowles:
I have yours of the 16th instant concerning the matter of holidays and sick leave with pay for charwomen working in public buildings throughout Canada.
Your representations have been carefully noted and will be given every consideration.
Yours sincerely,
Alphonse Fournier.
After some months, not having learned of any progress in the matter, I wrote the minister again, restating the case, but to my regret nothing was done. On February 25, 1944, the minister wrote me in part as follows:
The order in council you referred to-
I had referred to an order in council that had been mentioned in the daily newspapers. -does not cover holiday leave for the char staff. It applies only to full time and seasonal prevailing rate employees. As the charwomen are part time only they do not come under the terms of this order in council. This follows

Supply-Public Works

the practice employed in the industrial and the commercial world where holiday and sick leave are not granted to part time employees.
For your information, however, I may say that this whole question, together with others, is being reviewed by this department with a view to adopting some additional regulations covering sick leave in keeping with the kind of service performed by the different employees.
That also was signed by the Minister of Public Works. It may be that these women who do char work are employed on a different basis in different parts of Canada. That is my reason for bringing up this question to-day, in order that we may discuss it fully. It may be that the minister can point to some instances where they are employed on a temporary basis, but on a number of occasions I have consulted the women who do this work in Winnipeg; I have known some of them for a good many years, and I know that as far as their work is concerned it is of a permanent nature. I repeat, some of them have been employed there for as long as fifteen years. Their hours are set; the document I read referred to seven hours a day. Their remuneration is fixed on a yearly basis, and is divided into twelve equal amounts for the twelve months of the year. If these women lose any time because of illness they lose their pay, according to the number of days in the month in which that time is lost. It seems to me that if there are any little technical difficulties that have to be overcome the minister or the government ought to take steps to get around those difficulties in the interests of fair play as far as these women are concerned. Quite frankly, I have had the feeling that advantage was being taken of these women because of the nature of their work. They are rendering a real and very important service. Most of these women are working because of particular need. It. is by no means easy work. It is hard on their health. It takes them out at evening hours, which is by no means a desirable time to be working, and I think this parliament would want these women to be given every possible consideration. In my opinion their request that they be granted annual holidays of two weeks with pay, after they have worked a certain number of years, and a certain amount of sick leave without loss of pay is a most reasonable request, and I hope the Minister of Public Works and the government will find some way by which this can be done without' further delay.

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
The hon. member has certainly fairly stated the case of these women in Winnipeg. Under the public works department we have quite a number of charwomen
fMr. Knowles. 1
working in different cities throughout the country where there are public buildings. These women work from two to three hours a day up to seven hours a day, as in Winnipeg. In Ottawa there is a very large number of women working every day from six o'clock in the morning until eight-thirty, which is two and a half hours. They are part-time employees, although they also are paid on a yearly basis. In other places they work four or five hours a day, while in AVinnipeg there are thirty-five women working seven hours a day. I do not know if there are many cities in the country where we have women working that many hours. Representations were made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and we found that according to the labour regulations in Winnipeg holidays were given to these people if they worked forty-four hours a week.
In this instance they worked' forty-two hours. I have submitted this special case to treasury board. They have asked questions with respect to the labour regulations in Winnipeg. A few days ago I secured copies of those regulations and I am sending -the results of my inquiries to treasury board. I feel most sympathetic in this matter because it is a kind of borderline case. Had they worked two more hours a week they would have got the holidays as a matter of course. As the hon, member has said, this is a technicality, and I believe some redress should be made. I am expecting treasury board to deal with the matter in the near future, and I may tell the hon. member that I haive made recommendations to the effect that they get these holidays, as they are had in other trades.
I do not know if the same conditions would apply elsewhere in Canada. I believe this is a special case. There may be some isolated cases elsewhere, but they do not generally work the forty-four hours a week which would entitle them to- holidays. In this instance, however, hon. members may be assured that I will do my utmost to secure redress.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am grateful to the
minister for the statement he has just made, and I apprecate the sympathy he has expressed, and1 his willingness to do everything he can to cope with any technicality which may stand in the way. What he has said makes one feel that it was worth while to make the representations I did, and not to take the first "no" as a final answer.
I hold in my hand a letter sent to these women in Winnipeg by an official of one of the civil service organizations. This official had been in touch with the minister on a

Supply-Public Works
recent date, and the letter indicates that the minister was showing sympathy for the situation. I am glad to learn of the recommendation he has made, and I certainly hope our friends of the treasury board will reveal themselves in this instance as hawing some humanity in their hearts.
There is one other point I should like to make in connection with the work these women are doing in Winnipeg.
Women everywhere; not only Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I welcome my hon. friend's interjection. What he is saying is absolutely correct.
They are too poorly paid and not taken care of, as the hon. member pointed out.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
My reason for confining my remarks to the women in Winnipeg is that I know the situation there very well. It is a good idea in this chamber-and I believe the hon. member has emphasized it-to talk of things we know about.
So far as their cleaning work is concerned, I understand these women are supposed to clean so many thousand square feet a night; I am not sure as to the measures used. The regulation, however, is laid down in Ottawa. I am informed that the superintendent on the job in Winnipeg or, in fact, in any other city, has no authority to vary that regulation. This produces considerable difficulty and unfairness in connection with the work these women do.
In one instance a thousand square feet of floor space may require five or ten times as much work as a thousand square feet somewhere else. If one happens to get an open stretch of plain, ordinary floor, that would be a totally different story from having to clean the same amount of floor space on which there are desks, cabinets and other office furniture. For example, I am told one of the members in the cabinet has an office in a public building in Winnipeg. Naturally, because of his duties here in Ottawa, he does not go to Winnipeg very often. The result is that the woman who has his office in her allotment of floor space has a break, so far as that office is concerned, because it is not used much and does not require much cleaning.

Would that be an
Ontario cabinet minister?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
No; but now that I have
referred to the minister, perhaps I should
mention that it is my hon. friend from Manitoba, the Minister of Mines and Resources.
In taking this matter up with their superintendent, and pointing to him the inequality of the work they are called upon to do, I am told the women have been advised that nothing could be done, because the regulation had been issued from head office to the effect that each woman must clean so many thousand square feet. It seems to me that difficulty might easily be taken care of if a little more authority and responsibility were given the superintendent on the job. Would the minister give consideration to that point?

I do not often hear complaints about working conditions of people working for my department. I do not believe we treat them harshly. We have set down certain regulations with respect to the work they are to do in working hours. Really, however, in the two years I have been in the department I have not heard that they were given too much work. In Ottawa we have about 1,700 charwomen, and I have never heard that they complain they have been given too much space to cover. They may be given a thousand square feet to cover in two or three hours; I do not know what the time is. But they do not wash those floors every day. Sometimes they just come in and see that everything is in order, and kept clean.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Oh, I think they do their work all right.
Yes; they are all good working people who are employed. We would not keep them if they were not. And I would not want to hear any exaggeration as to their conditions of work.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I think the minister has missed my point. I am not complaining on their behalf as to the total amount of work the entire group has to do. I am complaining about the inequality in the amount of work allocated to the women, owing to the fact that the superintendent on the job has no authority to divide it up on a basis of actual volume, depending upon the conditions of the floor space cleaned.
We will tell our superintendents to be just as fair as possible in dividing the work among the women.

I should like to make a suggestion to the Minister of Public Works which would tend toward efficiency, at least in Fort William. My suggestion would be that women cleaners receive the same pay
Supply-Public Works

as men. We have difficulty out there in keeping women on their jobs; they have been resigning. Men cleaners are placed under the jurisdiction of the civil service. Anyone who knows anything about the way women fix things up, and clean them, will know that they are much better cleaners than men ever were. At least they should receive the same pay as the men. If they work overtime these women should be paid double time or time and a half, just the same as the men. I think the suggestion is most admirable and it would make for harmony and happiness among these women who are cleaners.

I should like to say a word with respect to the employees of the Department of Public Works and I join in a general way with the hon. member for Fort William. I had thought that by now this government would have put into operation the policy which has been enunciated so many times in this house, that of equal pay to men and women for equal work.

You announced it yourself.
Mr. GRAY'DON: Yes, but perhaps my powers of conversion have not been as powerful as they would have been had I been allied with the hon. member for Fort William who supports the government. However, I did not rise to discuss that matter at this time. I wanted to refer to the uniform coats which have been furnished to the elevator operators in the parliament buildings and other public buildings in Ottawa. To me they are scandalous, and I think the Minister of Public Works will be the first to agree with me in that. I am ashamed to belong to a parliament that will provide that type of coat to men who are meeting the public from time to time. They should be provided with good serviceable uniforms for their work. Something should be done to prevent a recurrence of this kind of thing because it does not leave a very good impression upon the public, to say nothing upon the men who have to work in them.
I am sorry His Honour the Speaker is not at the moment in the chamber, but perhaps what I am about to say will serve as a notice to him of a question that I intend to ask when his estimates are before the committee. My remarks have to do with the protective staff of this building. I realize that the minister has nothing to do with these employees, but perhaps I may refer to them briefly. The protective staff of this building have had to go around in winter uniforms during the hot weather, and that is a national disgrace and a scandal. These men have to

meet the public and work when they are uncomfortable, and the whole situation is one which should be remedied.
With respect to the employees of the minister's department, I hope he will rise in his place and say that a great mistake has been made, that it was not done with his authority or approval. I should like to see the responsibility and blame attached to some one. Some one must be to blame for a condition like that. To some people this may seem to be a small point to raise, but it only illustrates .nefficiency in the department which must be rooted out. It should be rooted out by those whose job it is to root out such things; that is the opposition. I should like to see these men dressed in decent uniforms so that those who see them will know that the government are interested in their employees.

If the leader of the opposition had not used such violent words as "scandalous" and so forth I would have been 100 per cent of his opinion. The first time I walked into the House of Commons and saw those coats on the elevator men I was shocked. I inquired where they had found the coats, and the answer given to me was that when they had come to try to get the cloth for these coats, this was the best the puichaser could find because of the shortages. I am not an expert in these matters, but I fully agree that I would not force any man to wear a coat like that
Where did they get these coats?

They probably asked for tenders as we always do when we want to clothe our employees. They had to use the cloth placed at the disposal of the public, and this was the best they could find. I would not blame my officials to the point of saying that they had done something scandalous, but I did tell them that in the future they should try to find something more suitable and more presentable for public servants who are meeting the public in the capital city. I really hope next year when my estimates are up that these men will be better clothed.

I expect that the minister will be on the other side inquiring of someone in our group with respect to that. May I suggest that one reason for the situation is that plans were not laid far enough ahead to obtain coats for the men. I think the minister had better start laying his plans now in order to get some decent summer outfits, even if this matter may be under the supervision of another minister next year.

Supply-Public Works

I do not think these men have been supplied with complete suits; it is only with coats. I think that is one of the complaints they have been making, that they are not furnished with a complete uniform.

speechtext: Further to the question I asked, the minister was good enough to state that he had made a recommendation to the treasury board. I think I sent the first recommendation to treasury board about two weeks ago. On Monday or Tuesday I received a reply asking for details about the working conditions in Winnipeg and the hours worked, and I believe I sent a second recommendation to the treasury board yesterday.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The reply the minister received was not a declination; it was simply asking for further information?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister is following it through to the best of his ability?
Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is fine.

Chief architect's branch-
San. Ottawa-maintenance and operation of dominion public buildings and grounds, including rents, repairs, furniture, heating, etc., $2,9X9,480.

The committee probably is not aware of the actual situation in connection with this bridge, for it is one of the bridges that return revenue to the dominion government. It was built by the provincial government some forty-three years ago as a passenger, vehicle and railway bridge. A few years ago the provincial government decided to construct a new bridge, and since it was to be over a navigable stream they had to come to the dominion government for permission. Since the new bridge was to be just a few feet from the old bridge the question arose as to whether the old bridge would be a hindrance to navigation in the event that the new bridge was built. Following the controversy, the
Supply-Public Works

provincial government handed over this railway bridge to the dominion without cost. Three railways operate over the bridge, and pay tolls. My understanding of the matter is that the surplus accruing from the operation of the bridge each year was to be placed in a fund, and that if within ten years the dominion government did not take steps to put in a lift span to replace the centre span of the bridge, thereby removing the menace to navigation, the funds accruing over the ten-year period would revert to the provincial government. Time is getting along, and I should like to see some steps taken to remove this centre span and replace it with a lift span, thereby removing the menace to navigation and complying with the understanding or agreement entered into between the provincial and federal governments. Can the minister tell us the position of the fund now, and whether any steps have been taken to carry out the agreement?

We took over this bridge, I believe, on October 4, 1939. The agreement has ten years to run, and under it we are required to keep account of the revenues and expenses in connection with the operation of the bridge. Every year we make a report to the provincial government. We have ten years in which to decide whether we are going to instal this lift span. If we decide against doing so we are to return to the province the difference between the revenue and the expenses. We have five more years to go, and as yet we have not come to a decision in connection with this lift span.

Will the minister take steps shortly to have an investigation made into the matter? Some doubt was expressed at the time as to whether this centre span should be removed. Can the minister tell the committee the amount of money now in the fund?

I have not the details as to the amount of money we have in that trust fund. We will investigate the possibility of constructing this lift span, but our work is limited by the number of people we have out on the coast.

I rise at this time, not to discuss the matter of - the national gallery of Canada but to bring to the attention of the minister another matter which has gained considerable impetus and thought throughout Canada during the last while. At numerous teachers' conventions, educational organizational meetings and wherever people who are interested in literary and cultural pursuits have gathered together, resolutions have been passed and expressions of opinion offered in connection with the establishment of a Canadian national library.
I wish in a word or two to add my support to those expressions of thought. I have no desire to press the point at the moment. After all, we are in a war. Despite how encouraging the news may seem to appear at times, in all these things we must always keen our eye on the ball to the very last. What I am really advocating is that at the appropriate time-and there is always a right time and place for everything-there should be established a national library of Canada. I think it would be an indication that we have not in a new country forgotten the educational and cultural and literary side of life in our concern for things strictly material. I am quite sure that the government and those w'ho are kindly disposed to a suggestion of this kind would find a cordial response in the country generally. There is a widespread desire among the people for better facilities, better equipment and better opportunities to gain knowledge of the various subjects on which a library would be able to afford information. Undoubtedly our parliamentary library fills a great need; and when I speak of our library I think I voice the opinion of all in the house when I say that not only is it a great library in itself, but the services which are rendered by those in charge, including the parliamentary librarian, often make us w"rr! how they are able to accomplish the miracles of producing so promptly information that is urgently required.
Hear, hear. '

No; it does not come under this item.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
This item on page 38 of the estimates, with which we are now dealing, refers one for a break-down of the vote to page 177, and in that break-down I find mentioned a senior museum asssitant, other museum assistants, and a museum helper. It was because of those items in the break-down that I thought the museum was included in this item. At any rate it perhaps will be no
more out of order to make reference to the national museum than to a national library, and the minister might speak on that subject when he rises in a moment or two.
I think we all share the views expressed by the leader of the opposition that in these days, when we have found what we can do in the way of raising huge sums of money for the things that have to be done in the time of war, we should not forget to raise similarly large sums of money for the good things of life and for the cultural development of this country.
This is still one other activity I should like to mention which might be included along with this kind of work. It is strange that this item should come under the Department of Public Works, but that of course is no reflection on the minister; it is just a comment on the administrative set-up. Along with the national gallery, the national museum and the national library I would suggest that there is room in this country for the development of handicrafts. The suggestion has been made in some quarters that if a lead is to be given in this kind of work, it might come under this same division of the minister's department.
I should be glad if the minister would make some comment on the status of these things and at the same time state whether the government have any plans for enlarging the work of the national gallery and the national museum, and for setting up a national library, and instituting work in handicrafts.

Would the minister also give some information with regard to the purchase of pictures? I see that $15,000 of this sum is allocated to purchase the works of Canadian artists. From time to time the opportunity arises to become possessed of a work of considerable value, which would be a great addition to the national gallery, an opportunity which in the past has been considered one that should not be lost. I w'onder how the money is made available for such purposes.
Another thing I would ask the minister to go into is the extent to which the loan exhibitions have been made use of across Canada and where they have been shown.

In years gone by, the estimate for the national gallery was about double what it is this year. In 1928-29 the expenditure wTas $134,988.79. At the outset of the war the vote was cut down to $44,246.82. The estimate for 1942-43 was $43,082.44. This year it is increased to around $65,630. The increase comes about by the addition of two employees and the funds for the cost of living bonus. Since the beginning of the war a scheme was devised by the national gallery,
Supply-Public Works

and with the approval of the Minister of National Defence nearly ten thousand reproductions of the work of leading Canadian artists have been supplied to the Canadian forces at home and overseas for the decoration of recreation rooms and other quarters. At the request of the British war office two thousand prints have been distributed to the British forces. Two hundred prints have been sent to Canadian prisoners of war in Germany. The same prints have been supplied to United States units in Canada and Newfoundland, and are being furnished through the Department of External Affairs to all Canadian legations and government offices abroad.
We have held war-time exhibitions in Ottawa and elsewhere in Canada. The national gallery as a war service has made special efforts to hold exhibitions having relation to the war and the part of Canada and the united nations in it, beginning with the great "Britain at War" exhibition in 1941. The series has been continued with marked success, and has included Australian, Polish, Russian, Mexican, Czech, Chinese and United States collections, which have been shown first in Ottawa and subsequently circulated through Canada. A number of exhibitions of Canadian art have been held abroad and others are in process of formation or projected. The national gallery has placed its facilities at the service of the army and the Royal Canadian Air Force for the purpose of developing art exhibitions within the services. These exhibitions, which the military authorities regard as of the highest importance, involve a substantial amount of extra work on the part of the national gallery. The gallery also cooperates with the Y.M.C.A. in circulating art exhibitions to all camps in Canada.
As to educational work, the gallery has made special efforts to sustain public morale by increasing educational work in Ottawa and elsewhere in the dominion. Loan exhibitions have been improved and extended, and the musical programmes on Sunday afternoons have been made a regular feature of the gallery programme with good results.
As to the sale of reproductions by the national gallery, these sales increased to 14,8S6 in 1942-43 and to 26,000 for the first eight months of 1943-44, and probably reached a total of 30,000 before its conclusion.
I have an item here, "plans for future developments." A grant of S24.000 from the Carnegie corporation has been made available to the national gallery for the purpose of encouraging art interest throughout Canada, provided that the national gallery itself is able to make a fair contribution in this direc-

tion. Plans are now being made so that constructive action can be taken immediately peace is established.
There are two schools of thought. Many want us to increase this amount to a very high level, and I believe that in the next budget something will be done with that in view. As to the present time, the government is directing its efforts toward the conduct of the war, and it has not yet decided to increase our civil estimates in this direction. But I personally believe, with the leader of the opposition, that as a post-war project a national library would be a great memorial in a country of our size and population. I am not speaking for the government; I am giving only my personal opinion on this matter, but I think it would be one of the most useful ways in which we could spend the people's money so that they would have a return by being given the privilege and the opportunity of developing their knowledge and their culture. I would be prepared to second a proposition of this kind by the leader of the opposition if ever it came up for discussion.

I am not going to oppose a post-war effort for a national library, but to me there is something far more important than that. This war is being fought by all Canada. A national library placed in the city of Toronto or Montreal or Ottawa or Halifax or Vancouver or-
Fort William.

-Fort William, would help only one city. I think we should have a recreational centre in every community, with a reading room, with all the athletic endeavours of the community centred in that place. If you had that you could make it a memorial to our boys, and the government could very well give a donation. I am giving notice to the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Public Works that we shall count on the government of Canada for a donation of that kind, because they took our rink, and now it is one of the finest armouries in Canada, but we have no hockey rink. One of the outstanding agencies for the obliteration of juvenile crime is a recreational centre with a good reading room, with good, clean, Christian supervisors. It would far outshine any national gallery which could be put up in any centre in Canada.

Just to complete the record and be fair to the national gallery I should like to add this statement. In 1942 the director was made chairman of the Canadian war artists committee, established under the authority of the defence council to develop

Supply-Public Works
a record of Canada's part in the war, using Canadian artists. Fifteen of the foremost Canadian artists have been selected and commissioned-six in the army, six in the Royal Canadian Air Force and1 three in the navy. Some are in England, Africa, Italy and elsewhere as well as in Canada. The organization of their work, the supply of materials, the care of the paintings produced and the arrangement of exhibitions is largely the responsibility of the national gallery. An exhibition of Canadian war art will shortly be opened in the national gallery at London. As many qualified civilian artists as possible have been employed in Canada outside the defence council scheme under the direction of the national gallery. These artists have been assigned to work on the Pacific coast, the Alaska highway, the east coast, on the Atlantic convoys, and elsewhere to record important phases of Canada's war effort. In most cases the artists have contributed their time except for payments to cover expenses.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the minister indicate where the museum comes in the estimates?

These probably are the ones which take care of the paintings we have in the gallery. If the hon. member has reference to the museum, that does not come under my department at all. I believe it comes under-
Mines and resources.

I think it is an excellent idea to have these artists commissioned and securing for Canada some wonderful portraits and pictures of war scenes during the war. Has any thought been given to the method of housing these when they return? A suitable building will be necessary, and I suggest it might be well to think about that now. I remember that after the last war a great many important pictures were sent to Canada, and I am not sure that there is yet a suitable place provided in which to display them.
I understand we are giving thought to a project of that kind; but it is considered as a post-war project. We are not contemplating the immediate erection of a building in the midst of a war.

I should not think that
would be done now, but it will take some time to get ready for the post-war reconstruction period.

I support what my leader has said in connection with the national library. I would refer the committee to resolution which was passed in the other place not long ago with reference to a uniform school history bouk for Canada. In conjunction with a national library for Canada we could teach history on a basis that would be acceptable to all the provinces, and in that way we would do a great deal for the unity of the country.
