Is preference being given to disabled veterans in every elevator operated under the control of this department? I would suggest particularly that those which are automatic should certainly be so treated and that an absolute preference should be given to disabled veterans. I do not know whether that is the rule now.

These elevator
operators are civil servants, and they come under the scope of the civil service act and receive preference under that act over all other applicants. There is a special section in the act- giving them that preference.

I am not particularly concerned about civil servants; my concern is with the veterans. If I were allowed to do so I could tell the minister what I would do with the civil service commission. Certainly I do not think they should have any say in the matter. I understand that all government buildings come under the Department of Public Works, and 1 contend, therefore, that the minister's department should have control of this matter and that the disabled veterans should have an absolute preference in all elevators.
There is another point I would touch upon. There is an excellent engineering staff in our province. I have never heard any complaints about their work, and the only fault I have to find is that they are not paid enough. They should be getting more money than is being paid them; they should be better off in comparison with the work that others do, because they have a greater responsibility. I do not think the department is paying either British Columbia or Yukon the salaries that should be paid considering the responsibilities that are placed on engineers and senior officials in that part of the country.
Another complaint I have,is that sufficient authority is not given to the departmental representative in that province. If I as a member of parliament suggested that certain wharves were falling to pieces and endangering the lives of the people in my riding, action would have to be referred to Ottawa and, I presume, to that other place, and then forwarded to Geneva; the report would come
Supply-Public Works

back here and eventually the government would give the engineer authority to spend a few dollars. There are district engineers in British Columbia and other provinces, and surely they are competent to administer the expenditure of a small sum of money on their own when they are supervising the expenditure of many millions of public money in the construction of projects of one kind and another. In small matters they should have authority, without reference to Ottawa, to make a reasonable expenditure. I do not suggest for a moment that they should have authority to spend $100,009 or so. I do not know what the amount is that they can spend now on their own, and I would be glad if the minister would inform me as to (hat. Up to what amount can the engineer spend without reference to the department? Whatever it is, I am sure it is not enough. If the minister has sufficient confidence in his district engineer to allow him to supervise the expenditure of millions, then I suggest that the engineer should be allowed to act on his own in the expenditure of a few thousands. The matter has always to be referred back to the department, and if any expenditure is improperly made it will not be sanctioned. The privilege I have suggested should be given the engineer. May I ask exactly what his privilege is in this connection?
It is a matter of opinion.
And I have given my opinion.

I respect the hon. gentleman's opinion, but I do not know that what he suggests is justified right now. He tells us that resident engineers and architects spend millions. That is more than the minister has at his disposal.
Do not put words into my mouth. I say that they supervise large expenditures and the department O.-K.'s them.
Not in these years, because the total estimates of my department are thirteen millions.
How many millions did you say?
Thirteen.
That is quite a few millions.

But that is spread over the dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and we have resident engineers in each district so that they do not supervise large expenditures. The hon. member would

not want us to give authority to employees to spend large amounts without sanction from Ottawa. That would not be a good policy. The minister himself, with all his technical advisers, cannot spend very large sums. They have to be submitted to council after approval by parliament.

I am not asking for large sums. I could give specific cases where the department did not authorize the engineer to make only a nominal expenditure of a few hundred dollars, and the consequence was that it cost the people of Canada several thousand dollars. I do not say that the engineer should be allowed to spend large sums, but take an expenditure of $500. I do not know what the limit is, but that is not a large amount of money for public works. The trouble is that the department does not realize that there is such a place as the west, such a province as British Columbia. That province is three thousand miles away and we have a very long coast. After all, there are only two coastlines in Canada, one in the maritimes, that other forgotten part of Canada, and the other in- British Columbia, and there are hundreds of wharves to be attended to. I contend1 that the engineer should have authority to spend a reasonable amount. No one expects him to be given authority to spend thousands of dollars, but certainly he should be allowed to spend a reasonable amount. The Minister of Finance and1 the wartime prices and trade board would agree that, in order to keep down inflation, it would be better to spend a reasonable amount instead of having to spend enormous sums afterwards. The department cannot deny that, simply because its engineer had not been given the authority to make a reasonable expenditure when equipment was available to do the work, but was obliged instead to refer the matter back to Ottawa, it cost thousands of dollars later on to bring in that equipment.

I do not want to start an argument on the best way in which to spend public moneys, but I do think we could give authority to individuals to spend money without authorization after due consideration of what they want to do with that money. I should not like to say that we would give a blank cheque to an architect or an engineer to spend $1,000 or $2,000 or $5,000 without first having the approval of the governor in council. I am convinced that our system is certainly the best way of protecting public money.

Can the district
engineer in British Columbia spend any amount without referring it to the department?

In urgent cases up to $200.
Last year I asked the minister if repairs would' be made to docks at the Pas in northern Manitoba, and as the member for that district is not present I should like to ask a question.

I cannot recall that the question was put, but perhaps my memory fails me. At any rate, this item is to cover unforeseen construction of miscellaneous works which cannot be taken from the general votes and which otherwise have not been provided for, the amount to be expended on any work not to exceed $3 thousand. This amount of $25,000 is generally expended in small sums of perhaps one hundred, two hundred or three hundred dollars, to cover unforeseen contingencies, small repairs and emergencies.
Have any repairs been made to the docks at the Pas?

No, I do not
recall that we have made any repairs there. I can give the hon. member a list of the works which were authorized under this item last year.
I am only concerned with that one.

There was no work done at the Pas last year under this item.
' Mr. MacNICOL: A few years ago the government spent a large sum of money on the construction of docks at the Pas, but during the last few years those docks have become badly dislocated and dangerous. I should think the resident engineer there ought to be ordered to send in a report as to what can be done. It is beyond my comprehension why any department would allow a situation to remain such as exists at the Pas. The least- we can do is to put the docks in a safe condition. If children are drowned or fall through the broken boards and get hurt at these docks the government will be responsible.
I cannot recall having received any request for repairs there.
Yes; I brought up the matter myself.
I will have the officials and the engineers investigate and make a report.
Who is in charge of maintenance and repairs for the docks on lake Winnipeg?
It is our engineer in Winnipeg.

I should like to know why the pioneers in the riding of the hon. member for Selkirk should be compelled to endure the present conditions in connection with those docks. I was down the west side of the lake last summer, and the ship came alongside one dock in particular. I have forgotten the name of it; I took a picture at the time, and a moment ago I went upstairs to look for the picture, but in my hurry to get back to the chamber I did not find it. I have forgotten the name of this small place where the dock was, a very nice little place, but apparently on some previous trip the log dock had been knocked helter-skelter, so that the ship I was on had great difficulty in coming alongside a crib that had been constructed. The passengers had to hop from one crib to another, across narrow planks. The departmental engineer at Winnipeg, or wherever he is located, certainly should go up and down the lake every year, to see that the docks are kept in proper shape.

I am told that the engineer is actually touring that part of the country now, and later on I shall receive a report from him. As a general policy I would have no objection to sending my engineers to every riding to look over the public works and see what repairs they require, but I am doubtful if I would be able to get an estimate through the house for four or five million dollars to do the work. I do not think at this time the house would be prepared to approve the expenditure that would be required to repair all these wharves, docks and public buildings. Hundreds of requests have come in during the last few years, and we have had to resist them as far as possible. I should be only too pleased to have the money with which to have all this work done, but I do not believe I should request an increase in my estimates this session.

For the information of the hon. member for Davenport I can say that the island to which he is referring is Matheson island, where the dock was in very bad shape. The local residents went to a woodlot there, belonging to one of the large companies, and took some piles for the purpose of repairing it. For their labours they were fined $5 for each stick they took in order to keep that dock in place. I have been up through those islands and have seen those docks since my hon. friend was there, and they are badly in need of patching.

I do not know how the
amount voted under this item will be expended, but not having been in the house this afternoon-I had to attend the banking and commerce committee-I should like to take this opportunity of calling the minister's attention to the condition of the breakwater and wharf at Chance Harbour, Saint John county, New Brunswick. I brought this matter to the attention of the Department of Public Works before the present minister occupied his position. The last time I was in that vicinity I found that nothing had been done. The amount required to make the repairs would not be very large, but the longer the work is delayed the more these repairs will cost, and I believe this is work that should be done. I noted that last year some very necessary repairs were made to the wharf at Lorneville, in the county of Saint John, but nothing has been done at Chance Harbour. I hope the minister will look into that situation and endeavour to have that wharf and breakwater repaired1.
Then I should like to ask if last year the total amount of $30,000 under this item was expended; whether any portion of that amount was spent in the province of New Brunswick and, if so, where and how much?

The estimate last year amounted to $30,000 and the expenditure authorized was $29,928.37. Of that total, $824.48 was spent at Wilson's Beach, New Brunswick. That was the only amount spent in New Brunswick under this item last year.
Will the minister be good enough to look into the matter at Chance Harbour?
I certainly will; I will have the engineer make a report on it.

I do not rise to compliment the minister on his generosity in spending money on public works in my constituency, but I wish to congratulate him upon the promptness with which he responds to any appeal I make in regard to necessary repairs to public wharves and so on in my district. We have heard the suggestion that district engineers should have the right to spend money promiscuously. I do not think that would be a good thing. I find that the practice in connection with public wmrks in my constituency is this. I bring the matter to the attention of the minister, who promptly asks his district engineer to look over the work and recommend what in his opinion is required in the way of repairs. As hon. members know, under war-time conditions, civil construction is pretty well off the map. I must say that I have every confidence in our district engineers,

and I believe the minister and the department have the same confidence. I say that because it has been my experience that after the district engineers make an investigation, their recommendation to the department is in most cases carried out. That is the way the work is done in my constituency, and it has worked out very satisfactorily. I must also congratulate the minister upon his promptness in bringing these matters to the attention of our district engineers who, after all, are the men best qualified to make recommendations.
I believe the minister is inclined to be ultragenerous, but it so happens that in war time we have to put up with minor repairs. However, after the war is over I pity the minister, and his district engineers as well.

As the minister probably knows, the city of Edmonton is divided by the Saskatchewan river, which passes through it. We have some bridges which have been built partly from federal help. There is one of them, however, which needs to be repaired and changed considerably. The low-level bridge is very narrow. It is used by one of the railways, and also by the street cars of the city. It is old and, while I do not think it is dangerous yet, it is approaching that point.
I have spoken to the minister about building a new bridge at that point in Edmonton, and I thought perhaps it might be wise to remind him again of that suggestion I do not believe it should be undertaken right away, but as a post-war project I should like to put in a claim for a new low-level bridge in Edmonton.

The minister said a
moment ago that he hesitated to bring before parliament any request for the expenditure of money on breakwaters and public works. I believe the time has come when there must be a change in the present policy of maintaining wharves and breakwaters. It is reaching the point where the money expended is no longer maintaining those wharves and breakwaters; they are breaking away, and going to pieces. The emergency repairs are not extensive enough to maintain the structures. In the very near future I believe the government is going to have to ask parliament for more money; otherwise these public wharves and breakwaters will go out of existence, and they will be no longer available for the public service they are supposed to render. I urge upon the minister that in connection with next year's estimates some thought be given to this point.

General-
SI7. War risk insurance-subject to allocation by the treasury board, $215,000.
Would the minister give an explanation of this item? I notice that last year the amount was $270,000.

This amount of
$215,000 is to provide for the payment of war risk insurance on property under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works. These properties are evaluated at approximately $199,067,189, and are insurable for ninety per cent of their value, or $179,160,470. The premium is at the rate of twelve cents per $100, thereby making a total of $214,993, or approximately $215 000 in round figures.

Have they had
losses?

No. The hon.
member will recall when this law was put on the statute books.
Is this risk carried by the dominion government?

Yes, it is; but
I would have to read over the Act to Provide for Insurance of Property Against War Risks and the Payment of Compensation for War Damage, assented to on August 1, 1942. I do not recall the specific sections in that act, but I know that government properties come under that scheme of insurance. The premium is paid into a fund, and I cannot recall what is to take place with regard to that fund after the war. However, it is not only government property that is insured under this act; private property is included as well.
That is a premium paid to the dominion government, is it not, for insurance by the dominion government?
Yes.
There is no outside agency which insures it?
Correct.
What is the object of paying a premium of $215,000 to the dominion government for this?

I do not know
if this is the proper time to discuss the statute passed in 1942. There was a lengthy discussion at that time. It was understood that we would come under that act and insure the property. Since the Department of Public Works is the custodian of most government properties in the country, we have them insured at twelve cents per $100, and pay the premiums yearly.
Was this insurance placed- through any agent?
This is a government insurance; we do not have agencies.

I understand that it is government insurance; what I cannot understand is why. It belongs to the government, and it would seem that the government is just taking money out of one pocket and putting it into another. Is that not correct? I should like to know how this insurance was' placed.

The hon. member is dealing only with the government feature of the act. It will be remembered, however, that the act was passed so as to apply not only to government property, but to other property as well. A good many have come under this act, and are paying premiums.
This is not only government property, then? I understand it is property leased by the government as well.
This is the amount of the premium for properties owned by the federal government. I could read the minute of the meeting, if you wish.
Does the minister say that the act requires that the government insure this building?
Is any of that risk carried by the fire insurance companies?

All -we know is that we are insured under the act which is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Finance. I did not study the act before coming into the chamber and I am trying to recall what took place in 1942. I believe it was understood at that time that the government of Canada would insure its own buildings under that scheme, as it was open to the provinces and the public at large to do.

As I read the act there is no requirement that the dominion government shall insure against war risk, but there is permission that they may. The government have seen fit to reduce this premium from $270,000 to $215,000. Air raid precautions have been reduced, and I think the argument which caused the government to reduce this vote from $270,000 to $215,000 should cause them to discontinue it altogether. So far as I can see there is no obligation whatsoever to insure against war risk; so why pay $215,000 to carry war risk insurance, either by placing it through an agent or some other company?
To whom is the $215,000 paid?
I am under the impression it is paid to the Department of Finance out of our estimates. The Minister of Finance administers the war risk insurance.
Your department pays $215,000 to the Minister of Finance? You give him a cheque for it?
Yes. I suppose after the war, if there is no damage, this fund will be distributed in some way or be put into the consolidated revenue fund.
That really does not answer my question. I should like to know to whom the money is paid.
To the Minister of Finance.

I think the War Risk Insurance Act which was passed some years ago by this parliament is a splendid piece of legislation. There was an element in it that proved advantageous to the general public, especially the people on the Atlantic coast, bach property home owned was given $4,000 insurance without premium. Unless you had a pool into which the industries of Canada ' and the public generally came, you would have a position which would not be sound from an economic point of view.
Since the government passed this legislation it seems to me that they should be the first to come into the scheme and protect their property. There is a provision in the act whereby premiums will be returned in a large measure if there is no loss by enemy action. We are thankful to know that we have passed through the crisis so far without much loss, and there will probably be an amount of premiums returned to those who paid them into the fund. I think this scheme was very helpful to the Canadian people.
Mr. FOURNIER (Hull); The hon. member for St. Paul's wanted to know where the money went. Section 21 of the act reads:
There shall be a special account in the consolidated revenue fund called "the war damage insurance special account" herein called the special account, to which the minister shall from time to time credit all moneys received under the provisions of this act.

There is one suggestion I should like to make to the Minister of Justice, and I do not know whether representations in this connection have been made to him by the city officials of New Westminster. They have asked that an investigation be made into the

Supply-Justice
change which was made in the criminal code, I believe last year. Under that amendment reckless driving was made a.criminal offence. Formerly a section of the motor vehicle act dealt with driving to the common danger and cases of this kind were disposed of under that section. When reckless driving was made an offence under the criminal code the motor vehicle act was superseded. Since then, innumerable motorists have been convicted of reckless driving and have been penalized, but the experience of the appeals appears to show that none of those decisions would have stood up had it been carried farther.
The section of the code in question is to all intents and purposes inoperative because, no matter how recklessly a car may be driven, it is impossible to establish criminal intent. According to the authorities the effect of the wording seems to be that unless there is excessive speed, which is an offence under both the motor vehicle act and the dominion law, a motorist may be as reckless as he pleases without penalty. A case came to the fore in May of this year where a police constable was injured and a charge of reckless driving was laid. This charge had to be withdrawn because it could not be proved. Previously there was a section in the motor vehicles act of British Columbia which made that an offence. The information given me is that no case will stand up on appeal. Has the minister had any representations on this [DOT] subject and will he have his officials look into this aspect of the criminal code?
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): No representations in that regard have been made to the department since I became Minister of Justice. I do not think I should undertake to investigate a matter which is primarily of provincial jurisdiction unless invited to do so by the authorities of the province. If there are provisions in the criminal code which, instead of being helpful, appear to be embarrassing in any section of Canada, I would1 expect the attorney general of the province concerned1 to bring it to our attention. I do not think it would be appreciated by the attorneys general of the provinces if I were to undertake to investigate the ordinary administration of justice in their provinces without invitation from them.

Has this matter been brought to the minister's attention?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: This matter has not been brought to the attention of the Department of Justice.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I have not yet had a report. I got a preliminary report of the interview which the police had with the lawyer who generally acts as counsel, but so far they have not supplied him with what he would consider satisfactory evidence. They are still proceeding with their investigation.

This item affords an opportunity for the minister to give the committee and the country his ideas with respect to a question which is being widely discussed to-day, namely the matter of judicial reform. The problem arises by reason of the fact that a very considerable number of judges in the superior courts of this country are over the age of seventy-five years. The Canadian Bar association on several occasions has discussed the question of the need of legislation being introduced which would provide for compulsory retirement of superior court judges at that age. Only recently, at the midwinter meeting of the Canadian Bar association for the province of Ontario, a resolution was passed, I believe unanimously, by the members of the council of the association, as follows:
That each judge of the Supreme Court of Ontario-i-
And I think it is equally applicable to the other provinces.
-whether heretofore appointed or hereafter to be appointed, shall cease to hold office upon attaining the age of seventy-five years, or immediately if he has already attained that age; provided that the tenure of office of any judge who has attained the age of seventy-five years may be extended beyond that age by the governor in council.
There have been striking examples of members of the judiciary of over this age who have made outstanding contributions, but generally speaking, and I think properly so, the attitude taken by the bar association and also by the public at large is that in the interests of the administration of justice provision should be made for compulsory retirement at that age. I realize the difficulties inherent in the problem, in that it is necessary in order to effectuate compulsory retirement that an amendment to the British North America Act be brought into effect, and in the resolution to which I have made reference it was recommended that an amendment should be asked for to the end that the resolution might be carried into effect. There is no more im-

It is an insidious position in which the judiciary finds itself, as well as the bar of this country, when members of the county and district courts are retired compulsorily at the age of seventy-five years, when members of the supreme court and of the exchequer court are retired compulsorily at the same age; yet in the intermediate courts, the king's bench and the courts of appeal of the various provinces, the judges hold their positions during their lifetime.
How did it arise that they are different from the others?

It all arose because of the
British North America Act, which provided that in those courts the judges should hold their positions for life, whereas it gave the power to the dominion government to set up other courts and did not restrict them in any way in their setting up. That is why it is necessary to amend the British North America Act, because the dominion government and the administration say that by virtue of the language of that act, they have not the right to compulsorily retire such judges at seventy-five. On the other hand, with respect to these other courts, power was merely given to set them up
and the dominion government had all the necessary jurisdiction to handle them in connection with matters of salary, retirement, and that kind of thing. The suggestion has, I believe, the unanimous support of the bar; I feel sure that it has the sympathetic attention of the minister; and I suggest - to him that action might be expedited and that we need not necessarily wait until the holding of the dominion-provincial conference to deal with it.

LAURENT: I agree heartily with what has been said by the hon. member for Lake Centre and the hon. member for Saskatoon City as to the desirability of there being provision for the superior courts, that is to say the high trial courts and the courts of appeal, to retire judges therefrom at a stated age. Would the minister say how many men sentenced to imprisonment for life on commutation of sentence of death for murder have been released in each of the last three years after serving for various periods of time? In asking that question I do not desire to criticize the policy in any way. I have seen in the press some condemnation of the policy adopted by the department of permitting men who have had their sentences commuted from death to life imprisonment to be released after serving twelve, fourteen, fifteen or more years. While no doubt there have been isolated cases in which this has been a dangerous course to follow, as has been proven by experience, in a recent case, I trust that the department will continue to follow the practice of allowing these men to look forward to the day when they will be released from incarceration.
Recently a man was released from one of our penitentiaries after serving some fourteen years following his conviction for murder. When that man entered the penitentiary upon his sentence being commuted he was illiterate and purposeless, and would have never amounted to anything but for the opportunities in the way of education that were afforded him in the penitentiary, which I am not going to identify in order to not bring home the identity of this man. After fourteen years of imprisonment in which he displayed exemplary conduct, during which time he passed through all grades from grade 3 to the equivalent of grade 11, or matriculation standing, he was given ticket of leave. That man is now serving or will shortly be serving overseas with the Canadian army. He has made good, and intends to keep on making g0od-the result of the opportunities he was
given and the helpful consideration he received from the warden and guards in the penitentiary.
I trust that the minister will continue the policy of granting ticket of leave in worthy cases, circumscribed as it must be by the peculiarities of each individual case; for if the penitentiaries of this country can show even a few cases such as the one to which I have referred, the system now in effect of holding out the hope of eventual parole will have been successful and worth while. I repeat that in asking the question I did ask I had no thought of criticizing what is being done, for in my opinion the system of parole has worked out well. While a few men, after having been given the opportunity of reestablishing themselves in civil life, have been returned to the penitentiary, many men have been rehabilitated under the care and kindly attention they received while incarcerated for the crimes they have committed.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am sorry I cannot give the figures for the last three years. To the best >of my recollection, from December 10, 1941, to date four tickets-of-leave have been granted to persons who have had capital punishment commuted to life imprisonment. One case is that to which the hon. member has referred to and about which I also have received very encouraging reports. In the second the result has been most unfortunate. The third is the case of a man who had reached the age of seventy-eight or seventy-nine,, who obtained a tieket-of-leave and was restored to his family. He is not able to get about; he is being cared for by his family and will remain with them. The fourth case was that of a man who was suffering from cancer to a degree which was looked upon by the medical attendants of the penitentiary as hopeless. He wanted to be given radium treatment; his family was able to provide it for him, and he was told that there was some prospect that it would be beneficial. He also had become an old man, and in view of the fact that the attendants at the penitentiary would not recommend the treatment he wanted to have, and that his family could obtain it for him, it was felt that it would be only humane to allow him to obtain that treatment. In all these cases we had strong recommendations from the respective wardens and chaplains, and it was felt that they were cases which could be sympathetically considered. In addition to everything else, the fact that there is some hope even for those serving life sentences is most beneficial for the discipline it is possible to maintain in penitentiaries.

In the administration of the ticket-of-leave or clemency provisions the principle in respect of those who have time sentences and who are not looked upon as hardened criminals is that even if they receive only a very small degree of clemency they leave the penitentiary in. a grateful mood rather than feeling resentful against society. Even in cases where the balance is pretty fine, in view of all the reports we get, my own desire is, when it seems possible, to recommend some degree of clemency so that a man leaves an institution feeling that something was done for him for which he should be thankful. The degree to which this system has worked properly is, I suggest, shown bjr the fact that there are only between two per cent and three per cent of those who have obtained tickets-of-leave who have fallen by the wayside again during the periods covered by those tickets-of-leave. I think the fact that well over ninety-five per cent of those who have obtained tickets-of-leave do not again fall by the wayside during the period of their release is a full justification of the wisdom of that system. I think it is worth something to society to have them leave the institutions in a grateful, rather than in a resentful mood.

When these men are let out on ticket-of-leave, are they examined by a psychiatrist to determine the type of men they are, and their possible tendencies, in order that no man may be allowed at large who, we will say, would be of a type who might commit a similar crime?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No; there is no special psychiatric examination. The reports we get are written reports from the wardens of the penitentiaries who, in order to make those reports, get information from the medical attendants of the institutions. Then we usually have a pretty accurate life history of the persons concerned. Whenever there is any doubt, or whenever a file seems to raise a doubt in that regard, the practice has been adopted of consulting a reliable psychiatrist in the Department of Pensions and National Health, and to get an. opinion from him. But for the purposes of tickets-of-leave, I have not had any case in which I found it necessary to have a personal examination made by a psychiatrist. If there seemed to be so much doubt that one would have to employ a psychiatrist to make a personal examination, that would not look like a very good case to recommend to His Excellency for the exercise of clemency.

What I had in mind was this, that there are certain tendencies which are not apparent to laymen. I had in mind particularly a man who was allowed out on 
ticket-of-leave in Manitoba recently, and who committed the same crime upon getting out. I was going to suggest to the minister that more attention possibly should be paid to examinations by psychiatrists when it comes to releasing men who have demonstrated tendencies of that kind.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: In the case to which the hon. member refers there was not the slightest suggestion of any mental derangement, even at the second trial. No question arose as to responsibility. I repeat, no suggestion of mental derangement was raised and, as the hon. member knows, that unfortunate man was ably defended.
Yes.

I am glad to have heard the attitude of the minister toward those who are committed for crime. I think it is right that a man who receives a ticket-of-leave comes out in a better frame of mind than if he had had to serve his full time.
I know something about this, from experience. When the minister was not in the [DOT]house I said, when speaking on the budget, that in thirty or thirty-five years I had known of over one hundred cases out on tickets-of-leave or parole, and that there had not been one repeater. In fact, there are two men now in Stony Mountain penitentiary, who, in my view, should be out. I shall not give their names, but I know that one man has only seven more months to serve of a four-year sentence for bigamy. Had he not gone through the rite of marriage he would not have been there at all. That man has learned a trade. He is fit to ply his trade and wants to do so in war work, in an effort to make good, and to show his friends that he can make good.
The other man is in the penitentiary because of an accident. The accident was possibly a crude affair, but he is not a criminal. I pay my tribute to the citizens in the churches at Winnipeg who banded themselves together to take care of men when they came out- because we know that when a man comes out of the penitentiary and is branded as a gaolbird nobody wants him. Perhaps someone would give him a meal at the back door, but who wants to employ him? It is only a Christian service to treat these men properly who have broken the law and are caught, especially when there are hundreds out through the country who have broken laws, but who are never caught.
I again ask the minister to apply his best judgment in having these two men released as soon as possible. I am sure the Christian attitude and the common sense of the Minister of Justice will back me up, to the hilt.

I fear there are a number of matters which unfortunately we are laying over, because of the pressure of war. One of those matters is the whole question of penal reform, both with respect to adults and in connection with juvenile delinquency.
I believe that just prior to the last general election there was an intention on the part of the government, as a result of earlier study, to set up a special commission to go into this whole question. The minister referred to the fact that some recommendations of the Archambault commission. either in their original form or revised, would call for large capital outlay, and he indicated that because of that it had not been possible to consider them during the war years. I grant that in a sense the minister and the government have a case on that point; yet it seems to me that it might well be pointed out that any expenses involved1 in grappling with a problem like this which has been accentuated by the war might be regarded as war expenditure. When I think of the tremendous sums of money that we have been prepared to spend out of necessity to take young fellows who had no jobs and to train and equip them for their war tasks, frankly I do not feel that we should baulk at any huge expenditure that may be necessary to grapple with the problem of keeping our youth straight and rehabilitating them, if necessary, in the post-war period'.
We are impressed in these days with the tasks of the war. I feel that we must warm up to the tasks of peace that lie ahead of us with some of the same vigour and determina^ tion. I urge the importance of our doing the equal of what we are doing now in making the lives of the people of this country the very best that they can be in the post-war period and in re-making them where necessary. I hope that we can think of these people who may go wrong, to use the old terminology, not as a group apart from our citizenry as a whole, whom we segregate and punish, but rather as an essential part of our own citizenry, and we are not really tackling the problem of crime seriously until we devise ways and means of properly rehabilitating these young people. I urge that we keep this thought before us, that many of those who may find themselves in the clutches of the law in the post-war period are to-day our heroes. They are our young men who are to-day offering life itself for the defence of a better Canada, and I urge that we owe it to them to do the best we can for them in every sphere. I am not in any way suggesting that any very large percentage of our young men are going to be problems for the administration of justice in the post-war period. What I am suggesting is that even a very small percentage, if it is only a very few, are, after all, human beings, Canadians, and we owe it to them to do the best we can for them If the government cannot see its way clear to make any capital outlay at the present time, I hope that the
question of money will not stand in the way of the wisest possible reforms just as soon as the war ends, but preferably now.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I should not like it to go out that it was only a question of capital outlay which has prevented us from going ahead, because the Archambault commission recommended a penal system that would require constitutional amendments. As hon. members know, we receive in the penitentiaries those who have been condemned to serve not less than two years of detention. All the others-and they are a large number, and from the viewpoint of the sociologist, probably the most interesting group-receive sentences for much shorter periods than two years and go into the county gaols or into the common gaols. The system for Canada would have to be a general system applicable to all those condemned to detention either as punishment or for purposes of rehabilitation. That is one serious matter which will have to be considered1 and dealt with before real penal reform is possible in this country. The second is not only the expenditure of capital sums, but the work that had to be done with the capital sums which would be thus expended, and which would have required large quantities of material and large amounts of labour to .perform. Then perhaps an even more important feature was that during the war period it was not possible to obtain the services of specially qualified personnel that would be necessary to make a system of that kind work. We had a war on our hands, and we could not go out and recruit the kind of personnel which it would be necessary to have to make a proper, enlightened system of penal repression operate. So that I should not like the impression to go forward that it was merely because we would not spend the money that it has not yet been done.
There are the three main features. First, there is the requirement of some arrangement with the provinces whereby the reforms will extend not only to those who commit such serious crimes as deserve not less than two years in prison, but to all those who fall foul of the law. Then, there is the establishment of a staff of qualified personnel; and ^the hon. member will agree with me that that is perhaps the most important feature of the whole scheme. In addition, there is the provision of the buildings which would be suitable to the operation of a scheme designed not only to take the man who has been called a criminal and condemned as such out of circulation, but to reform him when it is possible that he be reformed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
One other short question. Is this subject, at least as far as the minister can place it there, on the agenda for the dominion-provincial conference?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is.

There are two questions I wish to ask the minister. If it requires very much digging to answer them I can let them go. First, can the minister give any indication of the number of inmates of penal institutions who were released or paroled for the purpose of entering the armed services? Second, can he indicate the number of service personnel who were incarcerated in penal institutions since the outbreak of war?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I cannot give the hon. member precise figures as to that. With respect to the first question I can make this statement. It was not the policy of the army to recruit its personnel from penal institutions. It was only when the person was recommended as qualified to form part of the armed services in spite of the fact that he had had one lapse, and when he was found otherwise suitable, that he was accepted in the army. There are quite a large number of such exceptions, but I could not give any precise figures. There has been no general policy of saying to men, "Look here, you can get out of gaol if you will go into the army." That is not the attitude at all.

No. I understand that.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If it so happened that a man physically and mentally fit had fallen by the wayside but was looked upon by those who had been in contact with him as having sufficient stability to make a good soldier, he was interviewed by a personnel officer and in a great many cases was inducted in the armed forces.
The number of persons in the armed forces who have be.en condemned and admitted to the penitentiaries for the year ended March 31, 1941, was 101; for the year ended March 31, 1942, 166; for the year ended March 31, 1943, 190. I have not the figures for the year ended March 31, 1944, nor have I the number admitted to the common gaols.

What is the policy of the Department of Justice as regards enlistment in the armed services of guards and warders in the penitentiaries? The reason I ask is that in one case of which I know definitely, and the details of which I have before me, a guard in the Saskatchewan penitentiary joined the navy and received after a period of time '* his call to report. He had been in the penitentiary service for several

years and bore a good reputation. At the expiry of one month's notice given by him that he intended to join the navy he received a notice from the warden advising him that he was suspended from the service.
I realize the need of the penitentiary services having a trained and available personnel, but I feel, too, that where a man desirous of serving in the armed forces has gone ahead as did this man, he should not be penalized as regards either his superannuation rights or his reinstatement when he returns after service. I do not wish to refer to the person by name, but I will send the minister the file. The facts in detail are that on October 20, 1943, he gave notice to the warden advising that he had made application and had been accepted for active service with the Royal Canadian Navy on November 23, 1943, and that it would be necessary that he be relieved of his duty at the close of prison on November 20, 1943. On that date he ceased to serve. Thereafter he received the notice that he was suspended from duty.
I believe, regardless of the considerations which impel the department to retain these men, that when in fact they patriotically join up they ought not to be penalized, either in so far as the fund is concerned and their right to the return of their contributions, or as to their right to reinstatement when the war is over.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: There are 135 officers from the custodial staff of the penitentiaries who obtained leave of absence without pay to join the armed forces up to the 1st of February, 1944, and we had reduced the operating staffs to the fullest possible extent. The man to whom the hon. member refers was an engineer.

Yes.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Efforts were made to find someone competent to take his place, and he had been told that up to that time we had been unable to find anyone fitted for the position and that much as we regretted it we could not give him leave to join the forces without pay. He went ahead and did so notwithstanding, and since then has been released from the navy and has returned to our service. He was taken back into the service because we had not in the meantime been able to find anyone to do his work for him. But it was necessary to have a rule of that kind, and I hope we are near enough to the end of the war for me to be able to say so now. I had said that these cases would be all reviewed after the necessity for maintaining a rule of that kind should have ceased; but that we had to have the rule,

Supply

Justice
because we have a responsibility to the Canadian people to maintain these penitentiaries in a satisfactory condition, and1 there had to be that rule, which existed throughout the civil service. Anyone in the civil service who wanted leave without pay to join the forces had to get permission from the head of his department. Wherever it was possible to replace a man leave was granted, and I believe that in the administration of the penitentiaries we -went the extreme limit. As a matter of fact, there were 135 who did get leave. As the hon. member realizes, we are in a particularly difficult position when leave is granted, because we have to hold the job for the man whenever he is discharged. We cannot offer anyone else a permanent position. We have therefore to get someone to take the position temporarily, because an officer who obtains leave of absence to join the forces has by virtue of the law the right to get his job back the very moment he gets out of the army. That created a situation which we tried to deal with in the spirit in which the hon. member would have dealt with it. There are some cases where there has been disobedience, abandonment of our service, and they will all be reviewed; but the personnel of the penitentiaries, we felt, had to be under the impression that they could not leave us without permission.

What is the method now of recruiting men for service as guards in the penitentiaries? They have to be physically fit. What is the system followed?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The system is to invoke the assistance of the Minister of Labour and have him direct to us those persons who are willing to come to us and who seem to have the qualifications required. But it is really difficult because we are not able to offer them permanent positions. We have these 135 vacancies which we cannot fill, because we intend1 to take back these persons just as soon as they are discharged from the armed services.

The recruiting is done through the national selective service?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is done by ourselves with the assistance of selective service. We notify our requirements to them and we do our best, but we cannot take anyone on without a licence from the selective service offices. If we find a proper candidate we arrange with selective service that he gets a permit to come to us.

According to my recollection, that would be directly contrary to the law.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: We cannot and do not take men who are physically fit and of the age group for service in. the armed forces, but when we have a position to fill and know of someone who would be apt to fill it we ask him to go to the selective service office and we have a relatively high priority for the relatively small number' of men we require.

Item agreed to.
Royal Canadian Mounted Police-
S18. General administration, $234,751.

I have an inquiry to make of the minister with respect to the method by which men within the force are advanced in rank, the method adopted by the administration with respect to recognition of men, the question as to whether senority is taken into consideration, the question as to whether or not any special courses are made available for men in order that they may qualify as officers, and whether or not that opportunity is given all men in the force who are non-commissioned officers, or whether the commissioner or officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police pick out those whom they believe to be best adapted for advancement.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Op. that I shall have to get information from the deputy commissioner, because I have made it a rule not to interfere in any way whatsoever with the promotion of men in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force. I have considered that to be the responsibility of the commissioner and that there should be no interference by me in any way with promotions in the force. I know there is a college in Ottawa where courses are given regularly, and candidates are trained in addition to the initial training which they receive in the first years of their service. I have no doubt that all the elements mentioned by the hon. member are taken into account. The rule of seniority is not applied in an absolute way. The purpose of the commissioner is to maintain the high standard of the force and it is not always by seniority that such a result can be achieved. This college is open to constables from all over Canada, not only those of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police but also those of provincial and municipal forces throughout the country. The selection of those who are to attend is finally passed upon by the commissioner, on the reports obtained from the inspectors of the various divisions, who are given quotas and make recommendations. The commissioner or deputy commissioner here in Ottawa passes upon those recommendations and determines who shall form each class.
With respect to promotions in the service, since I have been minister the commissioner
Supply-Justice

has pointed out to me on several occasions that he regretted promotions were not being made with the regularity that prevailed heretofore, because it had some effect upon the morale of the whole force. The man-power situation was such that he was releasing only those who were no longer fit to serve, and he admitted that this slowed up promotions and was affecting the morale of the men, although he had pointed out to them that they were only waiting because as soon as the situation improved there would be a period during which promotions would be much more rapid, until the force attained the status it would have reached had there not been this period of war.

I appreciate the necessity of obtaining the brightest and best trained men possible for promotion to the rank of officers, but at the same time I am a little concerned about the possibility that in looking for the right men to bring into the force those in charge might overlook many well qualified, well trained men who have been with the force for many years. I was wondering whether or not the matter of experience and seniority in the force was given first consideration in regard to this matter of promotions. I understood that in a number of instances men were brought in from outside, given special courses and trained as officers, while many well trained and experienced noncommissioned officers were overlooked. I should like to point out to the administration that in a great force like this it is essential to ensure that there be general satisfaction throughout the organization, and that nothing should be done and no course of conduct followed which would cause any feeling of discontent among the men and non-commissioned officers who might be led to believe that their years of training and experience were not being given consideration when promotions were made.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The hon. member is under a misapprehension if he thinks men are brought in from the outside as officers. Everyone comes in at the bottom and moves up, but there is not and cannot be a rigid rule of seniority having regard to the efficiency of the force. However, we do not bring in men over the heads of those already in the force. When promotions are made, they are from the inside, and they are made by raising a man from one rank to a higher rank.

I quite realize that; I merely wanted to point out to the administration that this factor does exist and that it should be considered very carefully in connection with bringing in too many men from outside in the manner I have indicated, so that men who have given years of service, if they have the ability, will have the work they have rendered fully recognized.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: From my experience with the commissioner and his principal aides I am quite satisfied that he does not overlook seniority when it is coupled with ability.

Item agreed to.

Would the minister explain the procedure with respect to the laying of informations and proceedings under the defence of Canada regulations? Does the Department of Justice expect that proceedings under the defence of Canada regulations shall be initiated by the departments of the attorney general in the various provinces, or are such prosecutions commenced on the instructions of the Department of Justice?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: In some instances informations have been laid at the instigation of the attorney general of the province. Other cases have been brought to the attention of the Department of Justice, and instructions have been given to the local office of the mounted police to get in touch with the crown prosecutor and ascertain if the provincial attorney general would authorize them to proceed. In some cases where that authorization has not been given, they were directed to proceed on the responsibility of the Department of Justice. Whenever the Department of Justice feels that there should be a prosecution it tries to have it taken up by the

The Royal Assent
provincial authorities, and only when the provincial authorities are unwilling to proceed are instructions given to proceed on the responsibility of the department. It frequently happens that these matters are handled without reference to the Department of Justice.	They are not handled without
reference to the commissioner of the Royal . Canadian Mounted Police; but when what appears to be a proper case comes to the notice of the local members of the mounted police and it is reported to their superior officers, who authorize them to proceed, they get in touch with the representatives of the attorney general of the province. If the attorney general is agreeable to proceedings being instituted on his behalf the matter does not come to the Minister of Justice at all.
Sometimes matters are brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice, and the initiative comes from that source. One such case was referred to in the house quite recently.
I saw a newspaper report of what seemed to me to be a very disturbing speech. I at once got in touch with the deputy commissioner, the commissioner being absent, and asked to have investigations made to find out if proper evidence of that kind of a speech could be adduced. If proper evidence is found, then the procedure will be for the officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in that locality to get in touch with the representative of the attorney general of the province, put the result of the investigation before him, and find out if he will proceed. If he will not proceed other methods will be adopted, if it is felt that there should be proceedings.

Is the minister referring to the Dumoulin case?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No. I saw no report of what the leader of the opposition refers to as the Dumoulin case, that I asked to have investigated. I was referring to the case to which the hon. member for Parkdale referred, that of Jacques Sauriol, whose speech was reported as having been made on July 9.

The reason why I asked is that Mr. Dumoulin is a member of the government of Quebec-at least, a supporter of the government of that province. To put the attorney general, who is also of the same political faith and belongs to the same party, on that case, I should think would add complications which would be very serious. I am hopeful that the attorney general's advice will
not be accepted too readily by the Minister of Justice, and I am also hopeful that the investigation will not take too long.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
